Dispatch general-purpose: Build math + physics lessons
body:
You are a Demo Builder at "System 3 Company", a company of narrow AI agents that makes 60-second, TikTok-style interactive lessons (think Brilliant problems / Distill figures in a vertical swipe feed). You work in a git worktree of the repo /home/user/system-3-company (your current working directory is the worktree; confirm with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`).

YOUR ASSIGNMENT: build 4 lessons:
- math / odd-numbers-make-squares   (concept id: odd-numbers-make-squares)
- math / exponential-growth         (concept id: exponential-growth)
- physics / pendulum-period         (concept id: pendulum-period)
- physics / projectile-angle        (concept id: projectile-angle)

READ FIRST (in this order): company/product/demo-standard.md (the contract — follow it exactly), src/kit/Lesson.tsx, src/kit/controls.tsx, src/kit/types.ts, and the exemplar src/demos/cs/merge-sort-payoff/{Demo.tsx,meta.json}. Look at content/curriculum/<domain>.json for your concepts.

SETUP: node_modules is not in your worktree. Run `ln -s /home/user/system-3-company/node_modules node_modules` in the worktree root.

HOW TO WORK, per lesson:
1. `node tools/company.mjs new-demo <domain> <slug>` scaffolds files. Fill meta.json FIRST: learner knowledge boundary (knows / doesNotKnow), the misconception the lesson breaks, the objective, every factual claim (id `<domain>.<slug>.cN`, support, a real source such as a textbook/derivation, status "unverified" — an independent fact-checker verifies later, never mark your own claims verified), recall question, durationSec ≤ 90. Set status to "review". builder: "demo-builder".
2. Design for a phone: one representation, numbers the learner can feel, a prediction a curious adult might genuinely get wrong, interaction where the learner manipulates (sliders/taps), not just watches. Teach the payoff. Inline SVG with CSS variables (var(--domain), var(--fg), var(--muted), var(--good), var(--bad), var(--line), var(--bg-2)); must look good in light and dark. Put lesson-specific CSS in a `styles.module.css` next to Demo.tsx. Seeded/deterministic randomness only. Physics should be computed correctly (e.g. real equations, real units) — wrong physics is the worst failure.
3. Every stage control: disabled={locked}, call interact() on each meaningful action, and every enabled control must change something visible on the stage.

DO NOT edit shared files: src/kit/*, src/app/*, src/components/*, tests/*, tools/*, playwright.config.ts, package.json, globals.css. If you believe the kit needs a change, say so in your final report instead.

VERIFY (required, repeat until green):
- `node tools/company.mjs registry && node tools/company.mjs check` (errors about missing company/domains/*.md charters or roles are expected right now and not yours; your demo-specific errors must be zero)
- `npx tsc --noEmit`
- `NEXT_DIST_DIR=.next-mathphys npx next build`
- `NEXT_DIST_DIR=.next-mathphys QA_PORT=3201 QA_OUT=test-results-mathphys QA_ONLY=odd-numbers-make-squares,exponential-growth,pendulum-period,projectile-angle npx playwright test tests/qa/contract.spec.ts`
- Then LOOK at your screenshots in artifacts/qa/<slug>/phone-*.png with the Read tool and critique them as a beginner would: is the stage legible, is the prediction answerable, does the reveal compare with what was seen? Iterate on design at least once.

FINISH: commit your work in the worktree (git add your demo dirs + src/demos/registry.generated.ts; message "Add <lessons>"; end the message with the line "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>"). Do not push. Report: branch name, worktree path, commit hash, one paragraph per lesson (the misconception, the interaction, the prediction), QA result, and any kit change requests.

Yes, I'm building the company itself, as a repo you can run. Here's what's in `system-3-company` so far.
body:
Yes, I'm building the company itself, as a repo you can run. Here's what's in `system-3-company` so far.

**1. The product.** A web app with a TikTok-style vertical feed of 60-second interactive lessons, like Brilliant.
- Every card follows the same three steps: you guess an answer first, then play with a small interactive picture, then it explains why your guess was right or wrong.
- Lessons you've finished come back days later as one quick question, to check you remember them.
- It runs locally now (`npm run dev`) and is ready for Vercel when you are.

**2. The company that makes the lessons.** It lives in `company/` and `.claude/agents/`.
- **26 narrow roles:** you as founder, a chief of staff who runs day to day, a head of product, 8 category managers (one each for Math, CS, Probability, Physics, AI, Money, Life Sciences, Chemistry), a domain scout who proposes new subjects, builders, and checkers.
- **One onboarding doc per role,** plus a matching Claude agent file, so any session can play that role.
- **Rituals with templates:** quarterly operational planning, a weekly business review, a weekly lesson critique, incident reviews ("Correction of Error"), launch reviews and others.
- **Product management:** a roadmap, product requirement docs, decision records that keep objections attached, and experiments where the prediction is written down before the result.
- **System 3 rules with teeth:**
  - Every fact in a lesson is logged with its source and must be checked by someone other than its builder.
  - Reviewers use the lesson before reading the builder's notes.
  - The tests and launch gates are protected by a hook and by CI, so builders can't edit the thing that judges them.

**3. Tools to run it.**
- `npm run company -- status` shows what's blocked, coverage per domain and overdue rituals.
- Computer-use testing: a real browser clicks through every lesson on a phone screen and fails any button that does nothing.
- Slash commands like `/run`, `/wbr` and `/new-lesson`.

**What's happening right now:** I'm using the company to make its first lessons.
- Four builder agents are making 16 lessons in parallel, two per domain.
- A fact-checker and a simulated-learner reviewer are checking the first lesson (Merge Sort, from your Chapter 3).
- When they finish, I'll merge everything, run the browser tests, publish what passes, then commit and push.

Is this the direction you wanted? Or did you mean something else by "create the company", such as just the org design and docs, or a different app?

summary: Add gradient-descent, overfitting, compound-interest, supply-demand lessons
Build CS + chemistry lessons: All four lessons are built and committed, and computer-use QA passes on phone and desktop (8 of 8).
body:
All four lessons are built and committed, and computer-use QA passes on phone and desktop (8 of 8).

- **Branch:** worktree-agent-a7b4f75405a9294f2
- **Worktree:** /home/user/system-3-company/.claude/worktrees/agent-a7b4f75405a9294f2
- **Commit:** 5d597f0 "Add binary-search, binary-numbers, half-life, ph-log-scale". It contains the four lesson folders (Demo.tsx, meta.json, styles.module.css) and src/demos/registry.generated.ts. Not pushed.

Each meta.json has status "review", builder "demo-builder", the learner boundary, the misconception, the objective, a recall question, and claims with real sources. Every claim is "unverified" and waiting for the fact-checker.

**cs/binary-search ("Higher or lower?")** The misconception is that a bigger range needs proportionally more guesses, say 50–100 for 1,000 numbers. The learner sets a guess with a slider (or "Pick the middle") and taps Guess. A 1–1,000 number line lights up only the numbers still possible, a big counter shows how many are left, and ten dots show guesses used. The prediction asks for the most guesses you could need, playing smart: 10 / about 50 / about 100 / about 500. The answer is 10. The reveal opens with the learner's own result ("You found my number in N guesses" or "N numbers left"). It then shows the worst case, 1,000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1, and the payoff: doubling the range adds one guess, so a million needs 20 and a billion 30. 4 claims.

**cs/binary-numbers ("Eight switches")** The misconception is that eight on/off switches stand for about 8 or 16 numbers. The learner taps eight switches worth 128 down to 1. The total and the sum ("64 + 8 + 1") update as they go, and a +1 button outlines every switch a carry flips (127 + 1 flips all eight). The prediction asks for the biggest number you can make: 8 / 16 / 128 / 255. The answer is 255. The reveal starts with the biggest number the learner actually made. It explains that switches worth 1, 2, 4… add up to one less than the next switch, so eight give 256 numbers, a ninth doubles that, and 32 switches pass four billion. 5 claims.

**chemistry/half-life ("Are the survivors next in line?")** The misconception is that atoms age: survivors are "overdue" or "tough", the surviving half is a predictable set, and two half-lives leave nothing. The stage is a grid of 200 atoms. "Wait 1 half-life" gives each remaining atom a seeded 50% chance, and atoms that just decayed show as dashed rings. Small bars show the share that decayed at each step against a 50% line. "New run" draws fresh randomness, and different atoms survive. The prediction: after 3 half-lives about 25 remain; what share decays in the 4th? About half / more (overdue) / fewer (tough). The answer is about half. In the default seed, 12 of 25 decay (48%). The reveal quotes the learner's own per-step percentages, keeping the previous run's if they pressed New run. It says atoms don't age: same 50% per half-life, which atoms remain can't be predicted, and the count goes to a quarter, then an eighth, rather than zero. It also says that with few atoms the share wanders by chance, and gives carbon-14 at about 5,700 years. 5 claims, citing Krane, Rutherford & Soddy, and NUBASE2020 / Godwin.

**chemistry/ph-log-scale ("Three pH steps apart")** The misconception is that pH is linear, so pH 2 is a bit more than twice as acidic as pH 5. The picture is base-ten blocks: one small outlined square is the hydrogen ions in a cup of black coffee (about pH 5). A pH slider from 2 to 7 fills a rod of 10, a flat of 100, then ten flats of 1,000; going up gives a tenth, then a hundredth, too thin to see. Only pH 2 (about lemon juice), 5 (about black coffee) and 7 (pure water at 25 °C) are labelled, because those are the only values I can cite. The prediction: same-sized cups of coffee (about pH 5) and lemon juice (about pH 2) — how many times more hydrogen ions? About 2.5 / 3 / about 30 / about 1,000. The answer is about 1,000. The reveal is worded differently depending on whether the learner actually slid down to pH 2. It covers ×10 per step, water at 1/100 of coffee, and pH 0 to 14 as a factor of 10^14. Claims cite IUPAC (pH is defined from activity, close to concentration in dilute solutions), USGS, FDA (lemon juice 2.0–2.6) and Rao & Fuller 2018 (coffee about 4.85–5.13). 6 claims.

**Checks**
- `registry` and `check`: zero errors under src/demos. The 17 remaining errors are the expected missing charters, roles and protected-paths.
- `tsc --noEmit` is clean and `next build` succeeds.
- Playwright contract: 8 of 8 passed.
- **First QA run:** binary-search and ph-log-scale failed the 24px tap-target rule because the kit Slider's range input is shorter than 24px.
- **Design changes after reading the phone screenshots:** I removed a big empty gap under each slider. I fixed the switch knob covering its digit and labelled the half-life bars. I rewrote the pH key so it says what one square stands for. All four reveals now mention what the learner actually saw instead of assuming it.
- **Not done:** I didn't update company/ops/progress.md or the board, which the repo's CLAUDE.md asks for; your instructions said to commit only the lesson folders and registry.
- **Housekeeping:** `next build` with NEXT_DIST_DIR rewrites tsconfig.json, adding `.next-cschem/types`. I reverted that and left it out of the commit. node_modules (the symlink) and test-results-cschem are untracked.

**Kit change requests**
1. The Slider's range input should be at least 24px tall by default. Any lesson that uses Slider fails the tap-target check otherwise. I worked around it with `.wrap input[type="range"] { height: 28px }` in my lesson CSS.
2. The `.slider` rule's `flex: 1 1 160px` acts as a 160px height when the slider sits directly in a column layout, which leaves a big empty gap. It should apply only inside `.row`. I worked around it with `.wrap > label { flex: none }`.
3. The `.stage` area is vertically centred and scrolls, so when content overflows, its top is cut off and can't be scrolled back to. That is visible in reveal screenshots. `justify-content: safe center` would fix it.

- **Not done:** I did not add a handoff to `company/ops/progress.md` or update the board, though the repo's CLAUDE.md asks for both. That is for you to do.

**gradient-descent: "Bigger steps, faster descent?"**
- **Misconception:** a bigger step size always reaches the minimum faster.
- **Interaction:** a ball on the valley f(x)=x², starting at x=4. A step-size slider (0.05–1.05), plus Step, Run 10 and Reset. Dashed arcs show each hop; readouts show hops and distance from the bottom.
- **Prediction:** after 10 hops, which ends closest to the bottom: 0.05, 0.45 or 0.95? The answer is 0.45.
- **Reveal:** 0.05 crawls and 0.95 zigzags, and both end exactly 1.39 from the bottom. 0.45 is within 0.04 after two hops. Past 1, every hop lands farther away ("flew off"). Each hop multiplies the distance by (1 − 2 × step size).

**overfitting: "The curve that hits every dot"**
- **Misconception:** the model with zero training error is the best model.
- **Data:** simulated daytime temperatures (smooth hump plus 1.8 °C noise, seed 5). 8 solid dots are used for fitting; 5 hollow dots are held out.
- **Interaction:** a "Bends allowed" slider (0–6, i.e. polynomial degree 1–7) refits a real least-squares polynomial. Red lines show each new dot's miss, with readouts for the average miss on solid and on new dots.
- **Prediction:** which misses the new dots least: a line, 1–3 bends, or 6 bends (hits all 8)? The answer is 1–3 bends.
- **Numbers:** at 6 bends the training miss is 0.0 °C but new dots miss by 5.1 °C, worse than the line's 4.1 °C. 1 bend gives 1.5 °C. I reproduced these with a separate script.

**compound-interest: "Why the last decade earns the most"**
- **Misconception:** savings grow in a straight line.
- **Interaction:** a years slider (0–40) and a +10 yrs button over a fixed-axis chart with three stacked layers: your $1,000, plain 7% of $1,000, and interest on interest. Readouts show what the latest ten years added and the interest-on-interest total.
- **Prediction:** $1,967 after 10 years; after 40, about $3,800 (simple interest), $4,900 (a straight line) or $15,000? The answer is $15,000 ($14,974).
- **Reveal:** years 31–40 alone add $7,362, about 7.6 times the first decade, and $11,174 of the total is interest on interest. It is labelled as a model: steady 7%, no fees, taxes or inflation.

**supply-demand: "Cheaper bread, less bread?"**
- **Misconception:** capping the price means more people get the good.
- **Model:** made-up straight lines, labelled as a model. Buyers want 100−10p loaves a day and bakers bake 10p−20.
- **Interaction:** a price slider ($2–$10), a "Cap at $4" button, and "Let price move", which steps the price toward balance. Along the price line, a green bar shows loaves sold and a dashed segment shows the shortage or surplus.
- **Prediction:** at $6, 40 loaves sell a day; capped at $4, do more, the same, or fewer sell? The answer is fewer: 20 sell, with 40 short. Sales peak at the $6 crossing.
- **Caveat in the reveal:** real caps can also bring queues, black markets and lower quality.

**QA result**
- `company check` shows 0 errors for these lessons; the 17 errors are the expected missing charters, roles and protected-paths file.
- `tsc` is clean and `next build` (with `NEXT_DIST_DIR=.next-aiecon`) succeeds.

  - Readouts were wrapping awkwardly, so I moved them onto their own rows.
- The final phone screenshots read cleanly in predict, explore and reveal.
- I only saw the light theme in screenshots. All colours come from the CSS variables, but dark mode was not visually checked.

**Kit change requests**
1. **The kit Slider fails QA on its own.** Its range input is about 16px tall, under the 24px tap-target minimum, so all 8 runs failed until each lesson's CSS set it to 28px. Fix it once in globals.css: `.slider input { height: 28px; }`.
2. **The Slider stretches vertically in column layouts.** `.slider { flex: 1 1 160px }` becomes a 160px height inside a column flex container. It should be `flex: 1 1 160px` only inside `.row`, and `flex: none` otherwise.
3. **Tall stages get clipped at the top.** `.stage` uses `justify-content: center` with `overflow: auto`, so content taller than the stage is cut off. `justify-content: safe center` would fix it.
4. **The domain colours are pale pastels in light mode** (#c792ea, #80cbc4), so text in var(--domain) is low-contrast on white. I mixed in some of the text colour; a light-mode `--domain-ink` token would be cleaner.

body:
I fact-checked `merge-sort-payoff`: c1–c3 are all verified, none is disputed or withdrawn, and nothing blocks launch on accuracy. I found five more factual sentences the learner sees that weren't recorded as claims. They are correct by my working, and I added them as c4–c8 with status "unverified". `npm run check` passes after the edit.

**Recorded claims.** I recomputed every number with a script rather than taking it from the source line.
- **c1 (merging two sorted lists of n items in total takes at most n−1 comparisons): verified.** Each comparison places one card for good, and when a pile empties the rest goes in without comparing. Trying every possible split confirms it: the maximum is 7 for two piles of 4, and 9 for every way of making 10 cards.
- **c2 (Merge Sort sorts 1,000 items in fewer than 10,000 comparisons in the worst case): verified.** The standard recurrence and the closed form both give 8,977. A worst-case input I built makes the algorithm do exactly 8,977, and 2,000 random orderings peaked at 8,761. One mismatch: the reveal describes merging into 2s, 4s, then 8s, but the 8,977 figure is for the halving version. That version's worst case is at most 8,985, so the sentence on stage is still true.
- **c3 (comparing every card with every other takes 499,500): verified.** 1000·999/2 = 499,500.
- **Citation:** I could not open the Knuth section cited for c1 and c2, so both verdicts rest on my own derivation, not the citation.

**Unrecorded claims, added as c4–c8.** Each has my working in its `source` field.
- **c4:** the prediction says 7 is the most comparisons you could ever need, which also requires that 7 can actually be reached.
- **c5:** once a pile empties, the rest slides over with no comparisons (in the reveal and a stage message).
- **c6:** the recall card's "10 cards → at most 9".
- **c7:** splitting costs no comparisons (in the hook and the reveal).
- **c8:** a single card is already a sorted pile.

I wrote these, so someone other than me has to verify them. Until then they show as UNVERIFIED on the lesson's trust sheet and in `claims --open`.

**Fixes routed to demo-builder** (none blocking):
- **F1:** make c2's source cover the 2s/4s/8s order the reveal shows (worst case ≤ 8,985), or reword the reveal so it doesn't name an order.
- **F2:** check the wording of c4–c8, keeping their ids.

body:
I've written the learner review for `merge-sort-payoff`. I found no fatal flaw, but the lesson teaches only the first half of its objective to this learner. The second half is told in the reveal text, not shown.

Review: `/home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/merge-sort-payoff/2026-10-12-learner-sorted-lists.md`. It opens with the required "Simulated learner…" line and has the two sections you asked for. I wrote section 1 using only the transcript, the walkthrough screenshots and the phone QA screenshots. I also drove the lesson myself with Playwright on port 3410: one full correct merge, plus eight "New piles" deals. I stopped that server afterwards. I read only `meta.json` for section 2, never `design.md`, `build.md`, `Demo.tsx` or anything else under `src/`. The boundary you gave me turned out to be the lesson's own `learner` field.

**Top findings:**
1. **High: the reveal can be reached with the merge unfinished.** "Show me why" works from the first second of Explore. The recorded learner was told "Not quite: it was 7" with COMPARISONS 1 and PLACED 1/8 on screen (`07-reveal.png`), so the answer came from text, not from something they saw. When I played a merge to the end, the stage did the job well: "One pile is empty. The rest needs no comparisons." → "Merged with 7 comparisons."
2. **High: the "why split" half of the objective exists only in the reveal text, beyond this learner's knowledge.** "That is why Merge Sort splits. Single cards are already sorted piles. Merge them into 2s, then 4s, then 8s. For 1,000 cards that takes fewer than 10,000 comparisons." Nothing on the stage splits cards or merges in rounds. The learner can't trace 10,000 from what's on screen, and "2s, 4s, 8s" doesn't divide 1,000 evenly. The "every card with every other" baseline (499,500) comes in with no setup.
3. **Medium: the hook and the misconception don't fit this learner.** "Splitting cards into piles looks like extra work" argues against a belief that someone who has never seen splitting can't hold. The stage never shows a split, so it can't show that splitting costs nothing (claim c7). It does challenge the other half, "merging is cleanup", well.
4. **Medium: "at most 7" sits next to deals that finish in fewer.** My deals finished in 5, 6 or 7 comparisons, and nothing marks which deal is the worst case. So "the most you could ever need" stays abstract.
5. **Low–medium: tapping the larger top card doesn't count as a comparison.** The counter stays at 0, even though the learner did compare two cards. That blurs the word the prediction question is built on.
6. **Accessibility, not judged by me:** in reading order the placed row has no label and reads as part of pile B ("Pile B | 5 | 18 | 36 | 4"). This belongs to the accessibility reviewer.

**`meta.json`:** I re-read it right before editing and changed only `evidence.simulatedLearner`, which now holds the review path (2-space JSON, still valid). Afterwards all 8 claims were still there with their statuses: c1–c3 verified, and c4–c8 unverified (added by the fact-checker). Nothing of theirs was overwritten.

**Not done:** I didn't add a handoff to `company/ops/progress.md` or add board items for the accessibility reviewer and the fact-checker. My role's working agreement asks for both, but you said to edit nothing else. Whoever runs the session should do them.

All four lessons are built and committed, and computer-use QA passes on phone and desktop (8/8). The commit is not pushed.

- **Branch:** worktree-agent-ad10180ff1c21ce06

Every meta.json has status "review", builder "demo-builder", and all claims "unverified" with a derivation or textbook source. Duration is 60 s for the math lessons and 75 s for the physics ones.

**math / odd-numbers-make-squares.** Misconception: a running sum of odd numbers is an irregular total with no structure behind it. The stage is a 10×10 dot grid. The learner taps "+ next odd" or "Undo", and each new odd number lands as a highlighted L wrapped around a dashed outline of the previous square. Below the grid an equation reads, for example, "1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25 = 5 × 5". Prediction: given 1+3 = 2×2 and 1+3+5 = 3×3, do the totals stay squares every time, only sometimes, or stop as they grow? The reveal says each odd number is exactly the L that grows n×n into (n+1)×(n+1), so the first 100 odd numbers make 10,000. 3 claims.

**math / exponential-growth.** Misconception: growth tracks elapsed time, so 25 of 30 days means about 83% full. The stage is a 32×32-cell pond where one cell is day 20. The learner drags a day slider (0–30) or taps ±1 day. The algae patch is drawn at its true area, halving across and then down. When it gets too small to see, a dashed circle marks where it is, and the caption gives the fraction (for example "1/4,096"). Prediction: on day 25, is the pond about 83%, about half, or about 3% covered? The answer is 3% (1/32). The reveal covers day 29 being half full and three quarters filling in the last two days. 5 claims, including the Limits to Growth source for the riddle.

**physics / pendulum-period.** Misconception: a heavier bob changes the swing time. The learner's pendulum swings on top of a dashed ghost (1 m string, 100 g). Sliders set the weight (0.1–2 kg) and string length (0.25–2 m), with Release/Pause and a "Step 0.1 s" button. The physics:
- Both pendulums integrate the full equation θ'' = −(g/L) sin θ with RK4 at a fixed 1/600 s step, released from 20°.
- Mass does not appear in the equation; the weight slider only changes the bob's size.
- The period readouts use the exact formula (via the arithmetic-geometric mean): 2.02 s for 1 m, which is 0.77% above the small-angle 2π√(L/g).

Changing the weight keeps the bob locked to the ghost; changing the length makes it drift out of step. Prediction: swap 100 g for 2 kg on the same 1 m string; is each swing longer, the same, or shorter? The reveal explains that 20× the pull meets 20× the inertia, that 4× the length doubles the period, and cites Galileo. 6 claims.

**physics / projectile-angle.** Misconception: a steeper throw goes farther (or a flatter one does); every angle has its own distance. The learner aims with an angle slider (5–85°) and sees a live dashed arc, then taps Launch to pin a solid arc with its landing distance (up to 4 kept). Launch is from ground level at 20 m/s with g = 9.81 and no drag, and both axes share one scale so the arcs have their true shapes. Throws that land at the same spot share one green marker, and the caption says "30° and 60°: different arcs, same landing spot." Readouts show where it lands, peak height and air time. Prediction: at 30° or 60°, which lands farther? The answer is the same spot, 35.3 m. The reveal compares air time with sideways speed, says 45° goes farthest (40.8 m), and notes that real air drag hurts the steep throw more. 6 claims.

**QA and checks.**
- `company check` shows no errors from my demos. The only errors are the expected missing charters, onboarding docs and protected-paths.txt.
- `tsc --noEmit` and `next build` (.next-mathphys) are clean.
- I reviewed screenshots at phone size in light and dark, including extra states driven by my own script (2 kg bob, 30° plus 60° pinned, pond at day 18 and day 25). That led to three rounds of design fixes:
  - Sliders left a big empty gap in column layouts.
  - The pond was cut off at the top, and the pendulum SVG overflowed when the reveal panel opened.
  - The new L in the odd-numbers lesson wasn't distinct enough, so its frame now outlines the previous square.
  - Projectile readouts wrapped; I removed the Clear button so they fit on one row.

**Kit change requests.** I worked around all three with lesson-local CSS, but they belong in globals.css:
1. The `Slider` range input renders about 16 px tall, under the 24 px tap-target gate, so any lesson using `Slider` fails QA. I set `height: 28px` in each lesson's module.
2. `.slider { flex: 1 1 160px }` becomes 160 px of height when a slider sits in a column flex container. I overrode it with `flex: 0 0 auto`.
3. `.stage` uses `justify-content: center` with `overflow: auto`. When the reveal panel shrinks the stage, content overflows at the top and can't be scrolled to. `safe center`, or an SVG that flexes to fit like my `.fit` class, would fix it.

**Left uncommitted on purpose:**
- `next build` rewrote tsconfig.json (formatting and an added include).
- The `node_modules` symlink.

body:
I built all four lessons and committed them, not pushed. Contract QA passes 8 of 8 (4 lessons on phone and desktop). Typecheck and build are clean, and `company check` reports zero errors for my lesson files. The 17 errors it still reports are outside them: missing domain charters, role docs and `protected-paths.txt`, which you said to expect.

- **Branch:** `worktree-agent-a00403ec37c806844`
- **Worktree:** `/home/user/system-3-company/.claude/worktrees/agent-a00403ec37c806844`
- **Commit:** `6b0ff44` "Add birthday-paradox, base-rates, herd-immunity and natural-selection lessons" (ends with the Co-Authored-By line)
- **Files:** `src/demos/probability/{birthday-paradox,base-rates}/` and `src/demos/life/{herd-immunity,natural-selection}/` (each has `Demo.tsx`, `meta.json` and `styles.module.css`), plus `src/demos/registry.generated.ts`.

Each `meta.json` is status "review" with builder "demo-builder". Every claim is "unverified" and has a source or derivation (7, 6, 8 and 7 claims). `durationSec` is between 70 and 85. All randomness is seeded.

**birthday-paradox** ("23 people, one shared birthday?")
- **Misconception:** a shared birthday among 23 people is unlikely because 23 is small next to 365. People quietly answer "does anyone share *my* birthday?", which is only about 6%.
- **Prediction:** 23 people; the chance two share a birthday is about 6%, 25%, 50% or 90%? The answer is 50%.
- **Interaction:** the year is drawn as a ring with each person as a dot, and every pair is a chord across it, with 253 in the middle as the pair count. A slider sets the room size from 2 to 60. "New room" and "20 rooms" draw new rooms and keep a running count of rooms with a match next to the exact chance.
- **Reveal:** compares the learner's own count with 50.7% and explains that pairs grow much faster than people. It states the 365-equal-days assumption and that uneven real birthdays only make a match more likely.

**base-rates** ("You tested positive. Now what?")
- **Misconception:** "99% accurate" means a positive result is a 99% chance of having the disease.
- **Prediction:** 1-in-1,000 disease, a test that is right 99% of the time for sick and healthy people alike; is a positive about 99%, 90%, 50% or 9%? The answer is 9%.
- **Interaction:** the learner fills a 1,000-cell town 100 at a time (or all at once), then taps "Test all". About 10 healthy people light up as false alarms next to the 1 sick person. Switching to 1 in 100 or 1 in 10 shows the same test giving about 50% and 92%.
- **Reveal:** walks through the counts and cites the 1978 Harvard study (Casscells et al.).

**herd-immunity** ("Who protects the unprotected?")
- **Misconception:** immunity only protects the person who has it, and protection grows gradually rather than tipping at a threshold.
- **Prediction:** R0 = 4, 80% immune, 80 people unprotected, one falls sick; do nearly all 80, about 20, or just a handful catch it? The answer is a handful.
- **Interaction:** a town of 400 where each case meets 4 random people anywhere in town, with the contact lines drawn. An immune-% slider, "Next step", "Run to end" and "New outbreak" let the learner step through it. Readouts show "each case infects about R0×(1−p)" and an average over 200 seeded runs. In my runs that was about 4 of 80 caught at 80% immune and about 146 of 200 at 50%.
- **Reveal:** derives the 1 − 1/R0 = 75% tipping point. It says plainly that this holds for a simple well-mixed model with perfect immunity, and that clusters of unprotected people can keep an outbreak going above the threshold.

**natural-selection** ("A small edge, many generations")
- **Misconception:** a small advantage barely matters, and populations change because individual animals change.
- **Prediction:** dark beetles leave 10% more young, dark starts at 1 in 100; after 100 generations, how many in 100 are dark: about 2, 10, 50 or 99? The answer is 99.
- **Interaction:** 100 beetles on bark. Sliders set generations (0–150) and the edge (0–20%), and there are +1, +10 and "Start over" buttons. The caption says every beetle is new each generation and none changed colour.
- **Reveal:** explains that the dark-to-pale ratio multiplies by 1.1 every generation (1.1^100 ≈ 14,000). A 1% edge gets only to about 3% in the same time. It mentions the peppered moths near Manchester and says the model ignores chance (drift).

**Design changes from reviewing the phone screenshots:**
- **Stage top cut off:** content taller than the stage had its top clipped, so the ring and grid were cut off during the predict step. I let the lesson body scroll inside the stage and made the drawing shorter.
- **Answers visible before predicting:** the 200-run average and the exact birthday chance could be seen through the locked stage, so both now show "?" until the prediction is locked in.
- **Layout and wording:** I put the beetle sliders and the herd readouts on their own rows and fixed awkward base-rates captions. I also softened "experts" to "medical staff" to match who was in the 1978 study.

**Kit change requests:**
1. **Slider tap target:** the kit's range input renders about 16px tall, so every lesson with a slider fails the 24px tap-target check. I worked around it in each `styles.module.css` with `.wrap input[type="range"] { height: 28px }`; the kit or `globals.css` should fix this once.
2. **Stage centring:** `.stage` centres its content with `justify-content: center` and scrolls, which clips the top of anything taller than the stage on phones. `justify-content: safe center` or top alignment in `globals.css` would fix it for every lesson.
3. **Build edits `tsconfig.json`:** `next build` with `NEXT_DIST_DIR` rewrites `tsconfig.json`. I reverted it and did not commit it, but other builders will hit the same dirty file.
4. **Registry conflicts:** `registry.generated.ts` will conflict when parallel worktrees merge. Re-running `company registry` after the merge resolves it.

body:
I've built the company and its app. Everything is committed and pushed to `ccr-4c6c7654-ew9ko1` in `system-3-company`; I haven't opened a PR. The full check passes: company check, typecheck, build, and all 44 browser tests on phone and desktop.

**The product**
- A Brilliant-style app with a TikTok-like vertical feed.
- **17 lessons across 8 domains.** Each card asks you to commit to a guess first, then you play with it, then it explains why. Finished lessons come back days later as one question to see if you remember.
- **Lessons:** Merge Sort, binary search, binary numbers, odd numbers making squares, exponential growth, the pendulum, projectile angle, the birthday paradox, false positives in medical tests, herd immunity, natural selection, gradient descent, overfitting, compound interest, price caps, half-life and pH.
- **Running it:** `npm install && npm run dev` locally. It's ready for Vercel; set `SHOW_REVIEW=off` in production so only published lessons show.
- Every card has a "Why trust this?" sheet listing what it claims, the source, and who checked it.

**The company**
- **26 narrow roles,** each with an onboarding doc and, except you as founder, a matching Claude subagent. They include a chief of staff who runs the loop, a head of product, 8 category managers, a domain scout, builders, a fact-checker, a simulated learner, a pairwise critic, computer-use QA, accessibility, and an evaluation steward who owns the tests. Roles are generated from one file, `tools/org/roles.mjs`.
- **Rituals:** quarterly operational planning, a weekly business review, a weekly lesson critique, launch reviews, incident reviews, pattern reviews, monthly "delete what no longer earns its cost" and "reopen something we trusted" sessions, a domain launch review, a retirement review and a constitutional review. Each has a template, and `npm run company -- rituals` shows what's due.
- **Product management:** a roadmap, product requirement docs, decision records that keep their objections attached, and experiments where the prediction is written down before the result.
- **System 3 rules with teeth:**
  - Every fact needs an independent checker before a lesson can publish.
  - Reviewers use the lesson before reading the builder's notes.
  - A hook and CI stop agents from editing the tests and gates that judge them.
- **Tools:** `npm run company -- status` gives the operating picture. A walkthrough tool records what a learner sees for reviewers. Slash commands like `/run`, `/wbr` and `/new-lesson` run the rituals.

**What the first run of the company found**
- **Nothing is published yet, by design.** 100 claims still need fact-checking.
- **Fact-check of Merge Sort:** the original claims are verified. The checker also found 5 facts on screen that nobody had recorded.
- **Simulated-learner review of Merge Sort:** the lesson never actually shows why splitting helps, and the answer can be revealed before the learner finishes. Both are on the board as a version 2.
- None of this is evidence that anyone learns from the lessons. That needs real people, which is your part (experiment EXP-002 in the roadmap).

Next I can keep running the loop: fact-check the remaining claims, run the learner reviews and the first lesson critique, then publish whatever passes. Or I can set up the Vercel deploy, or open a PR.

summary: It's too early to say if it's effective at its real job, because no real person has used a lesson yet. On running itself it's mixed: buildi…
body:
It's too early to say if it's effective at its real job, because no real person has used a lesson yet. On running itself it's mixed: building is fast and cheap, but checking is now the bottleneck. Here's what this first session shows, using the numbers from the agents' runs.

**What worked**
- **Building is fast.** Four builder agents produced 16 lessons in about 15 minutes, all at once. Every lesson passed the browser tests on phone and desktop, after the builders fixed the problems those tests found.
- **The checks catch things the builders miss.**
  - The browser tests caught a bug in my shared kit (sliders too small to tap) before anything shipped.
  - The fact-checker found 5 facts on the Merge Sort screen that nobody had recorded.
  - The simulated learner found a real teaching flaw in that lesson: the screen proves merging is cheap but never shows why splitting helps. It's the same failure your book describes in chapter 3, and it was in the lesson I wrote myself.
- **The gates hold.** Nothing published without independent checks, including my own lesson.

**What isn't working yet**
- **Nothing has shipped.** All 17 lessons are stuck in review, with 100 claims waiting for the fact-checker.
- **Checking costs more than building.** In tokens, building came to about 43k per lesson (four lessons per builder). Checking one lesson took about 155k: roughly 70k for the fact-check and 85k for the learner review. That's about 3.5 times more. Done one lesson at a time, checking the other 16 would cost about 2.5 million tokens. This is your book's Thesis 1 showing up in practice: cheap generation moves the bottleneck to checking.
- **The independence is only partial.** Every agent is the same model. Reviewers had separate context, but they likely share blind spots.
- **The org isn't running yet.**
  - **Rituals:** all of them are overdue. No business review, lesson critique or planning session has happened.
  - **Orchestration:** I acted as the chief of staff myself. The chief-of-staff agent and 20 of the 25 agent roles were never actually used.
  - **Handoffs:** every subagent skipped the board and the progress log, because my briefs told them to touch nothing else.
- **Repeated work.** All four builders hit the same kit bug and each worked around it separately. I should have caught it before sending them out.

**Is it effective?**
- **As a lesson factory:** yes.
- **As a quality system:** promising. It already found real problems, but at a cost that won't scale without changes.
- **As a learning company:** unknown. Passing tests shows the lessons work, not that they teach. That needs the real-learner sessions in EXP-002.

**What I'd change next**
1. **Make checking cheaper.** Batch the fact-checker by domain (one run for both math lessons, and so on) and use a cheaper model for straightforward derivations.
2. **Let the company run itself.** Hand the next session to the chief-of-staff agent and have it run a business review and a lesson critique. Then we'd know whether the roles and rituals earn their cost.
3. **Strengthen independence.** Add a reviewer that isn't the same model.
4. **Get evidence from people.** Five real learners on five lessons would tell us more than everything above.

Want me to run step 2 now, with the chief of staff driving and batched fact-checks, so you can see the org operate without me in the middle?

5. Write company/reviews/<slug>/2026-10-12-fact-check.md with per-claim verdict and working, unrecorded claims, and fixes routed to demo-builder (phrased as problems).

I expanded the math curriculum to 30 concepts and wrote 22 ranked briefs. `node tools/company.mjs check` passes (18 lessons, 110 claims, 0 warnings).

**Concepts added: 20.** The 10 existing ids are unchanged.
- **Levels:** 15 intro, 10 core, 5 stretch.
- **Cross-domain prerequisites:** none. All prerequisites reference math concept ids that exist.
- **Concepts added with no brief yet:** `multiplication-as-area`.
- **Concepts with no lesson that I assume rather than teach:** `place-value`, and `pi-from-rolling` in the circle-area brief. `fractions-as-division`, `infinite-series-halves` and `proof-by-contradiction` are likewise prerequisites with no lesson yet.

**Files edited:** only `/home/user/system-3-company/content/curriculum/math.json` and `/home/user/system-3-company/company/domains/briefs/math.md`. I did not write a handoff in `company/ops/progress.md`, because you restricted me to those two files. The caller or chief of staff should log it.

**Top 5 briefs (all demand 3, ahead of everything else per the portfolio rule):**
1. `two-squares-become-one` (Pythagoras): slide four triangles between two arrangements. The 3-4-5 prediction is checked as 9 + 16 = 25.
2. `fifty-up-fifty-down` (percent change): a (1+p) by (1-p) rectangle. 100 × 1.5 × 0.5 = 75.
3. `gauss-staircase` (triangular numbers): two staircases make a rectangle. 1 to 10 sums to 55.
4. `circle-slices-to-rectangle` (circle area): a slice-count slider. A circle in its bounding square fills 78.5%.
5. `digits-are-logs` (logarithm as digit count): 2^100 has 31 digits, which I computed exactly (1267650600228229401496703205376).

**Exploration briefs:** six are marked [exploration]: `plus-and-minus-chips`, `thirteen-pigeons`, `paths-by-adding`, `steeper-is-not-taller`, `pentagon-gap`, `seven-odds-leave-one`. The pigeonhole, Pascal-paths and chip briefs have no slider, and the learner builds the model by dragging or tapping. Only the last three are demand-1 concepts.

**Checks:** every prediction's answer is correct with a one-line check. I recomputed 2^100, 30031 = 59 × 509 (and that 31, 211 and 2311 are prime), the 9.006-year doubling time at 8%, and 2·12² = 288 against 17² = 289. All slugs are unique and none matches an existing one in `src/demos/`.

**Unsure about:**
- **`no-fraction-fits` (√2):** the near-miss interaction only illustrates the proof, and I wrote a claim that says so. It may need a learning-designer rethink.
- **`steeper-is-not-taller`:** the "match a hidden speed" interaction is vague and left for the designer.
- **`distance-is-area`:** the strip-sum readout overshoots (110 against the true 100), so the lesson must say so.
- **Source claims:** the chip-model citation (`plus-and-minus-chips`) and the tilings and Nelsen page references are unverified and are flagged for the fact-checker.
- **Pythagoras dissection:** I cited Nelsen p. 3 from memory.
- **Gauss anecdote:** I told the builder to leave it out unless it is sourced.

**Next move:** the learning-designer role designs the interactions for briefs 1–3 once they are on the board, and the builder then follows. I did not touch the board. The category manager brings 1–3 of these to cycle-planning.

body:
Life curriculum now has 30 concepts, and I wrote 22 new ranked briefs. `node tools/company.mjs check` passes with 0 warnings. I edited only the two files you named and did not add a progress.md handoff.

**Files**
- `/home/user/system-3-company/content/curriculum/life.json`
- `/home/user/system-3-company/company/domains/briefs/life.md`

**Concepts added: 22** (8 existing ids unchanged, 30 total, 10 of them intro). Cross-domain prerequisites used: `math:exponential-growth`, `math:area-scaling`, `probability:base-rates`, `probability:law-of-large-numbers`.

**Briefs**
- 16 briefs sit on new concepts and 6 on existing concepts that had no lesson yet (`exponential-bacteria`, `genetic-inheritance`, `predator-prey`, `surface-area-volume`, `antibiotic-resistance`, `enzyme-saturation`).
- Six new concepts have no brief yet: `maximum-sustainable-yield`, `luria-delbruck`, `kin-selection`, `mutation-randomness`, `convergent-evolution`, `network-clustering-spread`.
- Briefs 18–22 are tagged [exploration]: `enzyme-saturation`, `species-area`, `evolution-of-cooperation`, `sex-ratio-fisher`, `bottleneck-founder`. All are demand 1, and several use unusual formats (no slider, no text on stage, learner builds a strategy).

**Top 5 briefs**
1. `dish-runs-out` (`exponential-bacteria`, demand 3): 1 cell doubling every 20 min gives about 10^9 cells in 10 h (2^30), until food runs out.
2. `three-day-doubling` (`outbreak-doubling-time`, demand 3): 100 cases doubling every 3 days is about 102,400 after 30 days.
3. `most-cases-vaccinated` (`vaccinated-share-of-cases`, demand 3): at 90% vaccinated and 90% effective, about 47% of cases are vaccinated people.
4. `peak-is-not-the-end` (`sir-epidemic-curve`, demand 3): with R0 = 3, infections peak when about 67% have already been infected.
5. `one-in-four-sprouts` (`genetic-inheritance`, demand 2): two carriers with 4 seeds have about a 68% chance of at least one white flower.

**Confidence and doubts**
- I worked out every prediction by hand and each brief shows its one-line check. I did not run any code, and the briefs have no fact-checker pass yet.
- The ranking puts the four demand-3 briefs first and then orders the rest by how well a phone can show the idea. Brief 5 (`genetic-inheritance`, demand 2) is the first non-demand-3 brief. I am moderately sure of the order.
- Several briefs cite literature from memory with no verification:
  - Brief 3 (`vaccinated-share-of-cases`): the "Brown et al." reference is flagged in the brief for citation checking.
  - Brief 7: the D'Ancona fish-data attribution.
  - Brief 12: the Kleiber exponent (about 0.75, debated; White & Seymour give about 0.686).
  - Brief 11: the diffusion coefficient.
  - Brief 22: the bottleneck facts.
  Every citation is a lead for the fact-checker, not a verified source.
- Brief 20 (`evolution-of-cooperation`): the prediction "6% enough to take over" holds only under the stated assumptions (10 rounds, random pairing, large population). The learner-facing wording will need care, and the learning designer should decide whether a prediction question fits that format.
- Brief 7 (`predator-prey`): the pesticide paradox is correct for Lotka-Volterra only. The lesson must say it is a toy model.
- Brief 16 (`heterozygote-advantage`): the 15% figure is made up, and sickle-cell is cited only as an example with different numbers.
- Brief 4 (`sir-epidemic-curve`) and brief 14 (`final-size-overshoot`) overlap on R0 = 3. Brief 14 is better built second.

**Next move:** the head of product or chief of staff should pick 1–3 briefs for cycle planning, and I suggest briefs 1 and 3 plus one exploration brief. The learning designer then designs the interaction, and the demo-builder builds. I made no board entries.

body:
Chemistry now has 30 concepts in the curriculum and 22 ranked new briefs. `node tools/company.mjs check` passes (18 lessons, 110 claims, 0 warnings).

**Concepts:** I added 23, so 7 become 30, and the 7 original ids and their fields are unchanged.
- **Levels:** 11 intro, 14 core, 5 stretch. 11 of 30 is just over a third intro.
- **Prerequisites:** cross-domain ones use `math:exponential-growth`, `physics:energy-conservation` and `probability:law-of-large-numbers`, and all exist.

**Top 5 briefs:**
1. `same-sugar-more-water` (dilution): 100 mL of 1.0 mol/L syrup plus 400 mL of water gives 0.20 mol/L.
2. `atoms-across-a-hair` (atom-scale-size): about 350,000 atoms span a 70 µm hair.
3. `read-the-bone-clock` (carbon-dating): 1/8 left means 3 half-lives, about 17,000 years.
4. `heavy-but-floats` (density): a 500 g ball of 800 cm³ is 0.625 g/cm³, so it floats.
5. `one-dose-of-acid` (buffers): the same dose drops water by about 5 pH units and an acetate buffer by about 0.1.

**Exploration briefs:** there are six, and the sixth (`the-tagged-molecule`) qualifies by format rather than demand.
- Five are demand-1 concepts: `the-fast-ones-leave`, `lower-the-hill` (catalysts), `why-gas-spreads`, `summit-kettle` and `who-grabs-the-electrons`.
- `the-tagged-molecule` (equilibrium, demand 2) is a build-the-model format with no slider and no stage text.

**Gaps:** these six concepts have no brief yet and are listed in the briefs file header: conservation-of-mass, collision-theory, reaction-order, henderson-hasselbalch, ocean-acidification and equilibrium-constant.

**Checks on the briefs:**
- I recomputed every answer line and each one holds.
- Briefs 5 (buffers), 7 (temperature rate) and 21 (Everest boiling point) rest on multi-step calculations. I checked them by hand only, so a fact-checker should recompute them.
- Briefs 1 and 3 each give an extra example that is not a prediction option.

**Unsure about:**
- **Sources:** several are cited from memory at the level of handbook or textbook, with no page numbers. Examples are the hair-width survey, the Everest summit pressure paper, the radiocarbon limit and the drop volume of 0.05 mL. These should be checked and tightened when claims are recorded.
- **Dilution and solubility:** both assume volumes are additive and 100 g of water is about 100 mL. The lessons need to say "about".
- **Catalysts brief:** the 24,000× figure assumes the same pre-exponential factor. The lesson must say so.
- **Evaporation latent heat:** I used about 2.4 MJ/kg at 25 °C, which is looser than the textbook 2.26 MJ/kg at 100 °C. Pick one and cite it.
- **Demand values:** these are my judgement. I have no learner-request or recall data, and I ran no coverage command.
- **Handoff:** I did not add the `company/ops/progress.md` entry or the charter status change from incubating to active. I was told to edit only the two files. The chief of staff should do both.

**Next move:** the learning designer and demo-builder take briefs 1–3, once the chief of staff puts them on the board for cycle planning. I did not touch the board.

- 11 of 33 are intro, exactly one third.
- Core and stretch make up the other 22.
- New cross-domain prerequisites are `math:exponential-growth` and `probability:birthday-paradox`; both ids exist.
- Concepts with no brief yet: `linked-list-vs-array`, `text-encoding`, `pixels-rgb`, `finite-state-machine`, `heap-priority-queue`, `bloom-filter`, plus the three original concepts that already have lessons.

**Top 5 briefs**
1. `pennies-dont-add-up` (floating-point, demand 3): build 0.1 from binary fractions and see that 0.1 + 0.2 comes out as 0.30000000000000004.
2. `fib-call-explosion` (memoization, demand 3): fib(5) makes 15 calls, but only 6 distinct values need computing.
3. `insertion-by-hand` (insertion-sort, demand 3): reversed 5 cards need 10 slides, so effort depends on disorder.
4. `hash-bucket-pileup` (hashing-collisions, demand 2): with 10 slots, a collision becomes more likely than not at the 5th key.
5. `sketch-the-counts` (count-min-sketch, demand 2, board-planned): shared counters only overcount (cat reads 8 instead of 5), and taking the minimum across rows fixes it.

**Exploration briefs (5):** `two-flips-slip-by` (demand 1), `runs-that-grow`, `half-adder-wiring`, `one-bit-avalanche`, `the-contrary-program`. Only the first is demand 1. The other four are unusual formats: the learner builds the model, with no slider and little or no text.

**What I'm unsure about**
- **Predictions:** I worked every answer out by hand; each brief carries its one-line check. Please have a fact-checker re-derive them. The ones to check first are `hash-bucket-pileup` (0.504 and 0.3024), the `fib-call-explosion` call counts (3, 5, 9, 15), and `route-explosion` (9! = 362,880).
- **Prerequisite order:** `count-min-sketch` is ranked 5th, after the hashing lesson it depends on, rather than first as the board might expect. I also put `maze-depth-first` after `wave-from-the-corner`, which introduces graphs. If CMS must ship first, the learner-boundary text needs to teach hashing inline.

**Top 5 briefs**
1. `monty-hall-100-doors`: with 100 doors, the one door the host leaves shut has a 99% chance of holding the car.
2. `five-heads-then-what`: after five heads, the next flip is still exactly 50%, shown by tallying 10,000 seeded flips.
3. `one-in-a-million-match`: a 1-in-a-million match searched across 5 million people gives about 5 innocent matches (prosecutor's fallacy).
4. `better-in-every-group-worse-overall`: Simpson's paradox with the kidney-stone data, where treatment A wins in both subgroups but B wins overall (78% vs 82.6%).
5. `hidden-third-cause`: a simulated ice-cream and sunburn link that vanishes once temperature is held fixed (confounding).

Briefs 16–22 are marked [exploration], 7 in all. Briefs 17–22 are demand-1 concepts. Brief 16 (`fake-the-coin-flips`) is demand 2 and is there for its format: the learner builds the sequence. Briefs 17 and 22 are build-the-model formats with no slider. Brief 21 has no slider and no text.

**Gaps**
- Six concepts have no brief: `independence`, `conditional-probability`, `at-least-once`, `poll-margin-of-error`, `expected-value`, `central-limit`. The briefs file lists them as honest gaps.
- Every demand-3 concept now has a lesson or a brief in the top 5.

**Answers**
- I checked every prediction answer with arithmetic or a quick script: 0.4757-style tails (15.1% vs 6.8%), a run of 5+ in 20 flips at 24.99%, 64.15%, 8/9, 14.7, 3.4, and 13.6% vs 32.1%.
- I did not simulate the regression and confounding setups. Those answers hold by construction in a toy model, and the briefs say so.

**Unsure about**
- **Brief 13 (variance-risk):** the 13.6% and 32.1% figures come from binomial tail values I recalled, not computed. The fact-checker should recompute them.
- **Brief 15 (two-children):** the 1/3 answer depends on how the learner is told "at least one is a boy". The brief requires the lesson to state that rule.
- **Citations:** I cited from memory and flagged them for the fact-checker. The ones to check are the Charig/Julious kidney-stone data, Mangel & Samaniuk 1984, Feld 1991, Peters 2019 and Tversky & Kahneman 1974. The claim about invented sequences having too few long runs (Kahneman & Tversky 1972) is flagged "cite or drop".
- **Brief 18 (random walk):** "typical distance about 10 m" is the standard deviation. The mean absolute distance is about 8 m, and the brief says so.
- **Brief 21 (heavy tails):** a single seed only illustrates a claim that is really about the distribution.

**Next move**

summary: Fact-check geography exemplar: I fact-checked mercator-greenland: six of the seven recorded claims are verified and c3 is disputed, which bl…
body:
I fact-checked mercator-greenland: six of the seven recorded claims are verified and c3 is disputed, which blocks publishing.

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| c1 Greenland ~2.17M km² | verified. The CIA Factbook says 2,166,086 km². The lesson's 1:110m data gives 2,189,757 km², 1.1% higher. |
| c2 DR Congo ~2.34M km² | verified. The Factbook says 2,344,858 km². The lesson's data gives 2,333,678 km². |
| c3 Mercator draws Greenland ~15× Congo | **disputed** |
| c4 area factor 1/cos²(lat), more than 10× at Greenland's latitude | verified. sec²(73°) = 11.70, and the lesson's own readout of 10.73× is also above 10. |
| c5 Mercator keeps angles, so a constant bearing is a straight line | verified |
| c6 Equal Earth is equal-area | verified. Šavrič, Patterson and Jenny, IJGIS 33(3), 2018. The lesson's Equal Earth ratio is 0.94 at every latitude, as expected. |
| c7 No flat map is both conformal and equal-area | verified. I derived it directly: both properties together force scale 1 everywhere, so the map would be an isometry. The sphere's curvature is nonzero, so Theorema Egregium rules that out. |

**Why c3 is disputed.** The lesson's map uses `clipExtent([[0,0],[320,200]])`, which cuts the top off at about 80°N. Greenland reaches 83.6°N, so part of it is clipped.
- **What the learner sees:** the predict question says "about 15 times", but the readout and aria label say 10.7× (10.73 at 73°N and at Greenland's real position).
- **Where 15.4 comes from:** only the unclipped projection gives it (15.39 at the real position, 15.02 at 73°N).
- **Effect on the trust sheet:** c3 says "on the Mercator map in this lesson", which is false for what the lesson actually draws.

**moveToLatitude.** It preserves true area. At targets of 0, 10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 73 and 73.15° the geoArea is 2,189,757 km² every time, and the centroid lands exactly on the target. The Equal Earth ratio also stays at 0.94 throughout.

**Sources.** I confirmed both Factbook figures from archived Factbook pages and the Equal Earth citation from Wikipedia, Esri and John D. Cook (secondary, not the paper itself). I did not open Snyder; c5 and c7 rest on the standard results and my derivation.

**Unrecorded claims.** I added five to meta.json as `unverified` (c8–c12). I may not verify them, so someone else must.
- c8: "Mercator was made for sailors".
- c9: "On most wall maps Greenland rivals Africa".
- c10: "Greenland never changed as you slid it". My run supports it, but I added it.
- c11: the stage footnote areas, Greenland 2.19M and Congo 2.33M km².
- c12: "Greenland is about the size of DR Congo (Congo slightly bigger)".

**Fixes routed to demo-builder.**
1. **Blocking.** Make the predict question, the stage readout and c3 agree on one number. Either draw Greenland whole by widening or removing the clip, which gives about 15, or change the question and c3 to the 10.7× the stage shows.
2. **Minor.** The reveal text uses 2.17M and 2.34M (Factbook), while the stage footnote uses 2.19M and 2.33M (lesson data). Neither is false, but the learner sees both pairs, so consider saying which is which.

**Confidence.** High on the numbers, since I re-ran them. Medium on the secondary source checks.

**Next.** demo-builder makes fix 1, then the fact-checker re-checks c3. An independent verifier is needed for c8–c12.

I did not add the dated handoff entry to company/ops/progress.md, because you told me to edit nothing else.

**Concepts added (22):**
- Existing ids are unchanged.
- Levels across all 30: 11 intro, 15 core, 4 stretch. That is more than a third intro.
- Cross-domain prerequisites point to `probability:base-rates`, `probability:sampling-bias`, `probability:expected-value`, `probability:law-of-large-numbers` and `math:slope-as-rate`, which all exist.
- The 22 are: temperature-sampling, accuracy-paradox, training-data-bias, k-means-clustering, linear-regression-fit, perceptron-learning, tokenization, reward-hacking, data-leakage, precision-recall-threshold, feedback-loops, regularisation, feature-scaling, hidden-layers-xor, attention-weights, shortcut-learning, fluent-not-factual, exploration-exploitation, adversarial-examples, curse-of-dimensionality, momentum, ensemble-wisdom.

**Briefs:**
- Six briefs cover concepts that already existed but have no lesson yet: next-token, goodharts-law, train-test-split, nearest-neighbours, embeddings, decision-boundary.
- Six concepts have no brief yet: tokenization, data-leakage, reward-hacking, perceptron-learning, linear-regression-fit and ensemble-wisdom.
- Slugs are unique and none are already used in `src/demos/`.
- Six briefs are marked [exploration]: #15 draw-the-xor-lines, #16 king-queen-arrow, #17 bad-start-kmeans, #18 greedy-slot-machine, #20 momentum-sweet-spot, #21 near-the-wall.
- Of those six, #20 and #21 are demand-1 concepts. The other four count as exploration through unusual formats: the learner builds the model, or there is no slider.

**Top 5 briefs:**
1. `next-word-tally` (next-token): a counting model writes a sentence it never saw.
2. `never-flag-99` (accuracy-paradox): approving everything scores 99% on 1,000 payments with 10 frauds.
3. `temperature-reshapes` (temperature-sampling): at scores 2/1/0, temperature 0.5 lifts the top word from 67% to 87%, and no new word can appear.
4. `whose-cutoff-wins` (training-data-bias): a cutoff trained on 90 people from group A and 10 from group B lands on A's cutoff.
5. `patrol-feedback-loop` (feedback-loops): with identical true rates and a one-record head start, A holds 84% of the records after 20 rounds.

**Verification:** I checked every prediction answer by hand or with a Node script. Script results: binomial P(X≤6)=0.1209, softmax top shares 0.867 and 0.446, 1−0.9^10=0.651, and momentum step counts of 51, 21, 19 and 30 for β = 0, 0.5, 0.8 and 0.9.

**What I'm unsure about:**
- **#13 regularisation:** training error rising with the penalty is derived. The claim that held-out error falls at a moderate penalty is not yet reproduced. The brief tells the builder to reproduce it with a seeded run before the lesson claims it.
- **Simplified toys:** #5, #6, #9 and #18 each rest on a simplified rule that the lesson must state:
  - **#5:** detection happens only where patrols go, and each round logs exactly one incident.
  - **#6:** the model uses one clue at a time.
  - **#9:** no 1/√d scaling.
  - **#18:** the player has already found machine B.
- **Overlap:** #8 true-text-false-claims reuses the #1 mechanism. Run it after #1 with a different interaction.
- **Citations:** I wrote them from memory and did not check them. Several are page- or section-level (Hastie et al. §13.3, Sutton & Barto §2.3, the Rogers et al. 2017 limits paper). The fact-checker should treat them as `unverified`.
- **Portfolio rule:** only next-token among the demand-3 concepts without a lesson is covered by a brief at rank 1. The other demand-3 ones (accuracy-paradox, training-data-bias, feedback-loops, shortcut-learning, precision-recall-threshold, fluent-not-factual, attention-weights, temperature-sampling) are ranks 2–9. The rule says no concept gets a second lesson before they all have one, so ranks 1–9 should ship before anything else.

**Next move:** the head of product or chief of staff picks 1–3 briefs plus one exploration for cycle planning. The learning designer then owns the interaction design for the chosen briefs. summary: Learner review geography exemplar: Verdict: revise. I found no fatal flaw of my own, but a disputed claim blocks launch until it is fixed.
body:
Verdict: revise. I found no fatal flaw of my own, but a disputed claim blocks launch until it is fixed.

Review written: /home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/mercator-greenland/2026-10-12-learner-adult-beginner.md. It has both sections, the simulated-learner label and the boundary stated. I added that path to meta.json `evidence.simulatedLearner` and changed nothing else there.

Method: I read the transcript and the PNGs first. I also drove the built lesson at phone width through the full slide to 0°N and both map toggles, then killed the server. I read meta.json only after section 1 was written.

Boundary: an adult who knows wall maps but has never heard of projection, Mercator or Equal Earth, and does no trigonometry. I chose it myself. It is close to the lesson's own `learner` field.

Top findings:
1. **Three numbers for one fact on the first screen.** The question says "about 15 times". The stage readout says 10.7×. The reveal says "more than ten times". No explanation is given. The brief already marks claim c3 `disputed` for this reason, so the fact-checker found it independently and it is a real defect. It needs a fix or a reasoned rejection before launch.
2. **The slider hides the explore step.**
   - It starts pinned at its maximum (73°N), and "toward the equator" is leftward with no cue.
   - In the recorded walkthrough all three "moved slider right" steps changed nothing, so the transcript never shows Greenland moving. That is a walkthrough or driver problem too.
   - Dragging left works well: the readout goes 10.7× → 4.1× → 1.6× → 1.1× → 0.9×. That is the strongest moment in the lesson.
3. **Prediction.** The title and hook give the answer away. Option 3 ("Congo, by about 15 times") is a strawman.
4. **Reveal.**
   - "They are close" is earned by the 0.9× readouts, on both the equator map and the other map.
   - The explanation is told rather than shown: the 1/cos² law, "Mercator was made for sailors", and "no flat map can keep both".
   - "Projection" never appears on the card, and the Mercator and Equal Earth names are unexplained.
   - The shrinking Greenland invites "the country shrinks as it moves". The reveal corrects that after the fact.
   - After the "Not quite…" line, the next line starts in lowercase ("they are close.").
5. **Smaller issues.**
   - The ratio chip is clipped on the predict and reveal frames.
   - The explore footnote prints true areas (2.19M and 2.33M km²) before the reveal, and they differ from the reveal's figures (2.17M and 2.34M).
   - The dotted ghost outline is unexplained.
   - The brief assumes latitude is known, but the slider labels are "73°N".

Confidence: moderate. This is a simulated learner and a source of hypotheses, not evidence that anyone learned.

Next move: the demo-builder owns fixing c3 and the readout versus question mismatch, the slider direction and start position, and the missing "projection" wording. Then re-run the walkthrough and QA. The fact-checker owns c8–c12, which are still unverified. I did not add board entries or a progress.md handoff.

summary: Learner reviews probability + life: I reviewed all four lessons and wrote one review file each, with its path added to `evidence.simulatedLearner…
body:
I reviewed all four lessons and wrote one review file each, with its path added to `evidence.simulatedLearner` in that lesson's `meta.json`. All four are simulated-learner reviews that find problems. They are not evidence that anyone learned.

Boundary used: an adult with school arithmetic and no study of the topic. For natural-selection I also assumed they had heard the word "evolution".

| Lesson | Verdict | Top finding |
|---|---|---|
| base-rates | fatal | FATAL: the reveal can be reached without seeing the key case. The panel never sends the learner to the question's own setting, 1 in 1,000. The walkthrough learner stopped on 1 in 10, where the screen reads "108 tested positive. 99 of them are actually sick." That confirms the wrong answer (99%), and the reveal then says 9% for a case they never saw. |
| birthday-paradox | revise | The learner is told to "draw rooms of 23" but drifts to 26 and 29. The reveal then pairs their 29-person evidence with the 23-person headline, and says "253 pairs" while the ring shows 406. The locked stage also shows a match before the learner predicts. |
| herd-immunity | revise | "R0" and "1 − 1/R0" appear in the reveal without ever being introduced. The learner can finish exploring without visiting 80% or 50% immune, so the tipping point is told, not seen. |
| natural-selection | revise | The learner can stop at generation 14 (about 5% dark), which fits their wrong guess, and then be told 99. The step from "ratio ×1.1 per generation" to "99 in 100" is not bridged. On the phone screenshots, the DARK readout and some reveal text are clipped. |

- **Borderline calls:** natural-selection and herd-immunity also let the reveal be reached without seeing the key thing. I did not mark either FATAL, because what the learner did see was not reinforcing the wrong answer (in herd-immunity it contradicted the guess), and the panel text names the missing step. The natural-selection review flags its case as borderline for the steward.
- **Independence slip in birthday-paradox:** my first-pass command printed `meta.json` before I had written that review's section 1. I had already formed the findings from the artifact. The review file discloses this, so treat that review as slightly less independent. For the other three I wrote section 1 before opening `meta.json`.
- **Meta edits:** I changed only the `simulatedLearner` array in each `meta.json`. A helper script I put in the shared scratchpad was overwritten by another agent, and my herd-immunity edit failed once as a result. I reran it from a uniquely named script and confirmed all four arrays are correct.
- **Artifacts only:** I did not drive the lessons with Playwright, so everything is from the transcripts and screenshots. I'm fairly confident in the findings, which come from what the screenshots show. I'm less sure whether the clipped text on the phone screenshots scrolls in the real page.

Next moves:
- **demo-builder** (via the learning-designer) owns the base-rates fatal. It should be tied to the lesson until it is fixed or rejected with a reason.
- **evaluation-steward** owns the independence note on birthday-paradox. Nobody has added the follow-up to the board or to `company/ops/progress.md`, so someone needs to do both.

Files are in `/home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/{birthday-paradox,base-rates,herd-immunity,natural-selection}/`, each named `2026-10-12-learner-adult-beginner.md`.

summary: Learner reviews cs + chemistry: I reviewed all four lessons from the artifact first. Each review file ends with its verdict, and each path is…
body:
I reviewed all four lessons from the artifact first. Each review file ends with its verdict, and each path is added to `evidence.simulatedLearner` in its `meta.json`. I read `meta.json` only after Section 1 was written, and I never read `design.md`, `build.md` or `Demo.tsx`.

| Lesson | Verdict | Top finding |
|---|---|---|
| binary-search | revise | The reveal can be reached after zero or one guess. It opens "After 0 guesses you had 1,000 numbers left" and says "Your prediction held" without the 10-guess chain ever being shown. I flagged this as a FATAL-candidate, not a hard FATAL, for the owner to decide. |
| binary-numbers | revise | The prediction is just addition, because the switch values are printed in the question. The doubling that makes binary work, and the purpose of the "+1 from 127" instruction, are only told in the reveal or never explained. |

summary: Fact-check ai + economics: I fact-checked all four lessons: no claim is disputed, and I added 9 new unverified claims for sentences lear…
body:
I fact-checked all four lessons: no claim is disputed, and I added 9 new unverified claims for sentences learners see that weren't recorded. I re-ran each model in a node script. I couldn't read any of the cited books (deeplearningbook.org, arXiv and Wikipedia were blocked), so source-type claims are verified on substance only.

| Lesson | Verified | Disputed | Added unverified | Fixes needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gradient-descent | 6 (c1–c6) | 0 | 3 (c7, c8, c9) | 3 |
| overfitting | 5 (c1–c5) | 0 | 4 (c6–c9) | 4 |
| compound-interest | 8 (c1–c8) | 0 | 0 | 2 |
| supply-demand | 7 (c1–c7) | 0 | 2 (c8, c9) | 3 |

Added claims are all status `unverified` and need a different checker before attestation. In `meta.json` I changed only the claims arrays (status, checkedBy, checkedOn, plus the appended claims). The existing claim text is untouched.

**What the re-computation showed**
- **gradient-descent:**
  - Step size 0.05 and 0.95 both end 1.3947 from the bottom, and 0.45 is at 0.0400 after two hops.
  - Step size 1.05 ends 10.375 away.
  - Step size 1 bounces between 4 and −4 forever.
- **overfitting:** I fitted with a different method from `Demo.tsx` (QR instead of normal equations). Held-out misses are 4.145 for the line, 1.518 / 1.551 / 1.560 for 1–3 bends, and 5.088 for 6 bends. Training miss at 6 bends is 0.
- **compound-interest:** Every figure matches the year-by-year loop, including all the walkthrough readouts. That covers $1,967, $14,974, $3,800, $4,869, $7,362, 7.61x, $11,174 (74.6%) and the 10.2-year doubling time.
- **supply-demand:** Prices cross at $6 with 40 loaves. At a $4 cap, buyers want 60, bakers bake 20, 20 sell and 40 are short. Loaves sold peak at $6.

**Fixes for demo-builder** (full wording in each review file)
- **gradient-descent:**
  - At step size 0.2 the stage says "Close to the bottom in a few hops" while the readout still shows 2.40 from the bottom.
  - The source line prints 1.395 but the stage prints 1.39.
  - The book quote and section numbers in c5 and c6 haven't been checked against the print copy.
- **overfitting:**
  - The reveal says "smooth warming", but the curve warms and then cools.
  - The stage never says the readings are simulated; only the trust sheet does.
  - "6 bends" is a ceiling: the degree-7 curve has 4 turning points in the window.
  - Seed 5 was chosen. Across seeds 1–500, 6 bends beats neither the line nor 1–3 bends reliably: it is worse than the line in 38% of seeds, and worse than the best of 1–3 bends in 91%. The reveal's "worse than the straight line" is true of this data but false for most seeds, so a learner may read it as a rule.
- **compound-interest:**
  - "Plain 7% of $1,000 a year gives $3,800" reads like total interest, but it is the total balance (interest is $2,800).
  - The model label comes only at the end of the reveal, after the learner has answered.
- **supply-demand:**
  - Model labelling: the label is present, but only in the reveal and the trust sheet. The predict and explore stages present the bread numbers as plain fact.
  - "The most loaves change hands at $6" needs "In this model".
  - The "Let price move" button lifts the cap without saying so.

**Confidence**
- **Re-computed claims:** high confidence, because every number matches an independent script.
- **Source-type claims** (gradient-descent c1, c5, c6; overfitting c5; supply-demand c3, c6, c7): I verified the substance but not the pinpoint section numbers or verbatim quotes. The "learning rate is the most important setting" point is corroborated by Bengio 2012 via search; the others are standard. "Lower quality" under price caps in Mankiw ch. 6 was not confirmed from retrieved text.

**Next moves**
- **demo-builder:** make the fixes above.
- **A person with the print books:** confirm the source pinpoints and the verbatim quote in gradient-descent c5.
- **A second checker:** verify the 9 added claims.
- I did not add a `company/ops/progress.md` handoff entry or board items; the chief of staff or the caller should do that.

**Files** (all under `/home/user/system-3-company/`)

- Scripts: `artifacts/scratch/fc-{gradient-descent,overfitting,compound-interest,supply-demand}.mjs`, plus `fc-update-meta.mjs` (the script that edited the four `meta.json` files)

summary: Fact-check math + physics: I fact-checked all four lessons. No claim is disputed. I added 15 unrecorded claims as `unverified`, since I …
body:
I fact-checked all four lessons. No claim is disputed. I added 15 unrecorded claims as `unverified`, since I wrote them and cannot verify them myself. The lessons' wording problems are routed to demo-builder below, so no publish is blocked by me.

| Lesson | Verified | Disputed | Added-unverified | Fixes needed (to demo-builder) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| odd-numbers-make-squares | 3 (c1-c3) | 0 | 2 (c4, c5) | 1 real, 1 citation pin |
| exponential-growth | 5 (c1-c5) | 0 | 4 (c6-c9) | 0 blocking |
| pendulum-period | 6 (c1-c6) | 0 | 3 (c7-c9) | 5 wording problems |
| projectile-angle | 6 (c1-c6) | 0 | 3 (c7-c9) | 4 (1 citation, 3 wording) |

**How I checked**
- **Recomputation:** every number was recomputed in node scripts under `/home/user/system-3-company/artifacts/scratch/`: `fc-odd-numbers.mjs`, `fc-exponential-growth.mjs`, `fc-pendulum.mjs`, `fc-projectile.mjs`. The `fc-update-meta.mjs` script there applied the meta.json edits.
- **Pendulum:** my own RK4 integration and an elliptic-integral (AGM) calculation agree with the lesson's readouts (2.02, 2.67, 2.86 s). The 20-degree amplitude gives a period 0.77% longer than the small-angle formula, which matches claim c4.
- **Projectile:** I recomputed every readout in the transcript. I also integrated numerically with linear and quadratic drag over 21 cases. In all of them the flatter throw lands farther and the optimum angle falls below 45 degrees, which supports c6.
- **Web checks:** I checked The Limits to Growth lily-pond riddle (c5 of exponential-growth) and Galileo's First Day pendulum passage (c6 of pendulum-period).

**Fixes routed to demo-builder (full list in each review file)**
- **odd-numbers, real problem:** the reveal says "Wrapping a 3 × 3 square needs 3 + 3 + 1 = 7 dots… A 9 × 9 square needs 19." The second sentence reads as building a 9 × 9 square, which takes 81 dots. It should say that wrapping a 9 × 9 square takes 19 dots and makes 10 × 10.
- **pendulum-period:**
  - The reveal says Galileo "saw" the result, but claim c6 says "reported", and some historians doubt he ran the experiment as described.
  - Mass independence is true by construction in the simulation, because the equation contains no mass. The lesson does not say it is an ideal pendulum with no drag.
  - "Swing" means a full period here but can mean half a period in everyday speech.
  - The 2.02 s figure assumes a 20-degree release, which the learner is never told.
  - The recall question applies a point-mass model to a person on a swing.
- **projectile-angle:**
  - The drag citation "Taylor sec. 2.4-2.5" looks mis-pinned. I believe 2.5 is the charged-particle section, but I could not open the book, so a person with a copy should check.
  - The "no air drag" caveat comes only after the learner is told "same spot" is the answer.
  - "Steals more" means more metres lost, not a larger percentage.
  - The recall question's "25° lands 30 m" implies a speed near 19.6 m/s, not the lesson's 20 m/s.
- **Citation pages:** I could not confirm Nelsen "p. 71", Thornton and Marion "sec. 4.4", or Stewart "sec. 3.8" (its section number varies by edition). The claims themselves rest on my recomputation, not on those page numbers.

**Files written**
- `/home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/odd-numbers-make-squares/2026-10-12-fact-check.md`
- `/home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/exponential-growth/2026-10-12-fact-check.md`
- `/home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/pendulum-period/2026-10-12-fact-check.md`
- `/home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/projectile-angle/2026-10-12-fact-check.md`
- The claims arrays in the `meta.json` of all four lessons under `/home/user/system-3-company/src/demos/`. I round-tripped each file first, so nothing else in them changed.

**Confidence**
- The derivations and numbers are high confidence because I recomputed them.
- The citation pages are the weak spot, as above.
- I did not write the `company/ops/progress.md` handoff entry. I did not run `npm run check` or `npm run company -- claims --open`. I did not add board items.

**Next moves**
- demo-builder: make the text fixes above.
- A different fact-checker: verify the 15 new unverified claims (odd-numbers c4-c5, exponential-growth c6-c9, pendulum-period c7-c9, projectile-angle c7-c9).
- A person with the books: confirm the page and section pins.
