**Design changes and brief issues (decision: learning-designer for the first three, cm-chemistry for the fourth):**
- **most-collisions-bounce:** I left out the "aim B" control. Since A stays random, aiming B gives 1 in 4, not "every shot hits" as the brief says.
- **the-slowing-half-life:** a halvings slider replaces the "wait for half" button, so QA's two arrow presses reach the key state.
- **one-ml-of-steam:** the learner sets the share boiled instead of dragging the piston. At 1 atm and 100 °C the volume follows from how much has boiled, so a free piston would be wrong.
- **ten-to-one-buffer:** the brief says the marker sits "three-quarters of a tick below pKa", but at 1:10 it is exactly one tick (1 pH unit) below. I built it to the maths.

Fact-check done for 30 lessons in ai, chemistry and cs. `node tools/company.mjs check` passes (258 lessons, 1346 claims, 6 warnings). All 6 warnings are old disputed claims in lessons outside my scope, except the three chemistry ones, which I left alone. I did not commit.

- **Lessons checked (30):**
  - ai: copy-of-a-copy, flagged-means-what, line-stops-at-the-edge, loophole-lap-farming, meaning-without-the-word, near-the-wall, one-bad-label-knn, step-too-long, which-answer-wins, window-forgets-start.
  - chemistry: four-to-one-settles, heat-in-no-rise, most-collisions-bounce, one-ml-of-steam, point-one-is-26-percent, steel-wool-gains-weight, summit-kettle, ten-to-one-buffer, the-slowing-half-life, who-grabs-the-electrons.
  - cs: half-adder-wiring, list-doubling-copies, lopsided-tree, lru-eviction-order, maze-depth-first, pivot-lands-home, route-explosion, runs-that-grow, two-flips-slip-by, wheel-of-negatives.
- **Counts:** 132 verified, 0 disputed, 1 added. I re-ran each lesson's model code in node (extracted from Demo.tsx) and every number matched. I searched the Shumailov, NOAA, IPCC SROCC, Po & Senozan and Everest-pressure sources.
- **Added claim:** `ai.meaning-without-the-word.c5`, left unverified. The reveal says the model answers "only from what retrieval hands it". Real retrieval-augmented models also carry knowledge in their weights, so "only" overstates it for real systems.
- **Disputed:** none. I weighed a few close calls and verified them with a note in the claim's `source`:
  - `chemistry.summit-kettle.c1` says 0.31 atm for the Everest summit. That is the standard atmosphere. The measured value is 0.333 atm, which gives about 71 °C boiling rather than 69 °C. I verified it as "about" and recommend "about 0.3 atm". The cited West 2006 paper could not be found.
  - `chemistry.point-one-is-26-percent.c1` cites AR6 "virtually certain". The 0.1 pH drop actually rests on IPCC SROCC ch.1 and NOAA (8.21 to 8.10), so the source should change.
  - `chemistry.ten-to-one-buffer.c5` gives a 0.01–1 mol/L range I could not read in the cited paper. My own exact calculation shows an error of 0.07 pH or less across it, so I verified it as a rule of thumb.
  - `ai.meaning-without-the-word.c3` has a weak source, since the French Constitution does not name Paris. Britannica would do.
- **Not touched, and need an independent checker:** 8 claims added by an earlier fact-checker pass, which I did not verify because I may not verify what that role wrote. Their own notes already record the wording concerns, so the builders should act on them.
  - ai.background-shortcut.c5
  - ai.border-follows-point.c5
  - ai.clicks-not-value.c5
  - ai.draw-the-xor-lines.c5
  - ai.gradient-descent.c11
  - ai.penalty-on-wiggle.c5
  - ai.temperature-reshapes.c8
  - cs.sketch-the-counts.c6
- **Not touched:** the 3 chemistry claims already disputed (`heavy-but-floats.c5`, `same-sugar-more-water.c6`, `the-tagged-molecule.c4`), outside the "unverified" scope.
- **Records:** `/home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/<slug>/2026-10-13-fact-check.md` for each of the 30 slugs, with the claim table, evidence and wording recommendations. Edited files are `src/demos/{ai,chemistry,cs}/<slug>/meta.json` (claim status fields, plus short notes appended to `source`).

body:
Fact-check pass 2 is done. `node tools/company.mjs check` passes (268 lessons, 1392 claims).

Counts: 57 lessons checked (Part A's 9 listed claims plus probability/friends-have-more-friends c5, math/one-boss-moves-the-mean c5, math/one-recipe-for-sixty c4, economics/two-bets-split c7). All of economics, math, physics, life, geography and probability that had unverified claims were taken. That includes 10 physics lessons that appeared at 06:21 during the session (crate-wont-budge, dam-depth-not-width, elevator-scale, magnet-still-in-coil, river-crossing-time, seesaw-sit-closer, snowshoe-pressure, toaster-trips-breaker, two-tugs-right-angle, wire-eight-times). Outcome:
- 11 disputed
- 1 left unverified
- 0 claims added
- Everything else verified, with checkedBy fact-checker and checkedOn 2026-10-13 (about 255 claims)
I re-ran the Demo.tsx model code in node, including the kit shapes, SIR/SIRS and model.ts, and checked sources by web search. I did not edit Demo.tsx.

Disputed, one line each:
- ai/border-follows-point c5: moving one 1-NN training point only changes the spots that switch nearest neighbour, not "every spot around it".
- ai/clicks-not-value c5: in the toy, clicks = 20 − value (perfectly inverse), so "clicks and value look related" and "tracks the goal" are not what the stage shows.
- ai/draw-the-xor-lines c5: "a band" holds only for parallel lines. Non-parallel solving settings give two opposite wedges.
- ai/gradient-descent c11: the message "hops are tiny" fires at step sizes 0.15–0.19, where the first hop is 30–38% of the distance.
- ai/meaning-without-the-word c5: "answers only from what retrieval hands it" ignores parametric memory in real retrieval-augmented models (Lewis 2020). It is true for the toy only.
- ai/penalty-on-wiggle c5: at penalty 10 the curve loses to no penalty in 441 of 500 seeds, not always, and "nearly flat" is too strong.
- ai/temperature-reshapes c8: Peeperkorn 2024 reports a weak positive link between temperature and novelty, so a flat "not more inventive" is too strong.
- economics/two-bets-split c7: for 2–3 bets the only loss is the full −10%, so "the losses left are small ones" is false there.
- geography/fingernail-ocean c2: the question implies fingernails grow 2.5 cm a year; Yaemsiri 2010 gives 3.47 mm/month, about 4.2 cm a year.
- life/vaccinate-at-the-peak c3: the reveal says "most infections were still to come" at the peak. By day 19, 65% of the town is already infected and only 30% of the eventual 94% remains.
- math/rabbit-ratio c4: for the 3,1 start the second ratio (4.0) is farther from 1.618 than the first (0.33), so "closer each time" fails at step 2.

Left unverified: geography/half-of-humanity c1 (the UN WPP 2024 population table). population.un.org, data.un.org, Wikipedia and OWID were all blocked (403) from this session. Partial corroboration only; the lesson's conclusion (seven countries make 51.4%) holds under the rounded values.

Not blocking, but worth fixing (in the review files):
- friends-have-more-friends: c5 is verified, but already-verified c3 ("wherever friend counts differ") is false for disconnected networks such as a triangle plus a K4.
- horizon-ruler says "a few per cent" for refraction; it is about 8%.
- sieve-crossing-out: "Four sweeps clear a hundred numbers" is loose.
- throw-it-fast-enough: ISS speed is 7.67 km/s computed against NASA's rounded 7.8.

Ledyard 1995 and UL 489 were confirmed only through secondary sources.

Each lesson has a pass-2 section appended to `/home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/<slug>/2026-10-13-fact-check.md` (new files created where none existed). I added a handoff at the top of `/home/user/system-3-company/company/ops/progress.md` and two board items. Nothing was committed.

Counts: launch 13, revise 7, fatal 0.
Fatal: none. average-that-never-settles is the closest, because its chart reads as the opposite of its reveal.
Revise: average-that-never-settles, better-in-every-group-worse-overall, coin-gap-keeps-growing, drunk-walk-distance, hidden-third-cause, monty-hall-100-doors, plus-fifty-minus-forty.
Launch: the other 13.
Most common findings:
1. The reveal quotes numbers the learner never saw, or ones that differ from the stage.
   - drunk-walk: the reveal says 9.4 m and 21.4 m, the stage showed 7.3 m and 24.9 m.
   - coin-gap: the reveal says 25 and 80, the stage showed 16 and 86.
   - hidden-third-cause: the all-days correlation of 0.83 is only in the reveal.
   - monty-hall: the 99% figure is never seen unless the learner picks 100 doors.
   - plus-fifty: $13,150 never appears on the stage.
   - better-in-every-group: the flip point of 220 is not visited.
2. The mechanism is told, not shown, and terms are used before they are defined.
   - Mechanism told: the x0.9 pairing in plus-fifty, the host's knowledge in monty-hall, 0.95^20, the odds notation in which-coin, the square-root rules.
   - Terms: Cauchy and heavy-tailed, correlation, "typical" and the unlabelled log axis, "343" in the slider label, "significant" and "null".
3. Hooks or questions leak the answer ("Surely...?", "Can it still lose overall?", "Or is that backwards?"), and some stages are cluttered or ambiguous.
   - average-that-never-settles: the Cauchy lines funnel toward 0 and look like slow settling.
   - twenty-harmless-tests: the tiles stay tappable after the 1,000-batch run for no stated reason.
   - monty-hall: the stage is largely empty.
   - at-least-one-boy: the grid counts are unequal while the text says "equally common".
Caveats: the screenshot spot-check was partial. I opened the predict, an explore step and the reveal for armour and at-least-one-boy, and one or two images each for about 14 others. Section 1 for every lesson was written before I read any meta.json. I read only the learner field (knows/doesNotKnow) for section 2, because the brief key was empty. I did not open build.md. I read the version number from meta.json before writing, which is v1 for all 20.
Confidence: moderate. These are simulated criticisms, not evidence that anyone learned.
Next move: the Evaluation Steward or the builders should triage the 7 revise items. The reveal-versus-stage number mismatches are mechanical fixes and should go first.

Fatal: none. Nothing was found that is false or unfollowable.

Most common findings:
1. Reveal names a value or claim the explore never showed (about 20 lessons). Examples:
   - antibiotic-already-there: 0.1 resistant cells at 10 million.
   - one-in-four-sprouts: reveal says 42% for exactly one white, but the stage showed 49.
   - stale-case-counts: reveal says 252 at 4 days, never tapped.
   - saturated-enzyme: 91 and 50 busy enzymes.
   - waves-return: waves are never shown, and the reveal's 50.0% disagrees with the stage's 50.7%.
   - strategy-builder: the 21f+9 equation is never built from anything on screen.
   The mechanism or "why" sentence is usually told rather than shown.
2. Hook, title or answer options give the answer away or lean on it (about 12 lessons). Examples:
   - five-day-generations
   - most-cases-vaccinated
   - same-genes-different-drift
   - keeping-the-bad-gene: the option "settles near 13%" is the answer.
   - strategy-builder: the 5% and 7% buttons bracket the answer.
3. Terms are used before they are defined, or the question is too dense (about 10 lessons). Examples:
   - spreaders-are-rare: "negative binomial, dispersion k" appears in the question.
   - cut-the-island: the exponent.
   - hidden-carriers: "squared" and the "CARRIERS EACH" label.
   - saturated-enzyme: a packed question and "versus half as much".
   - epidemic-overshoot, waves-return, pockets-below-threshold: R0.

Other recurring items:
- Reveal and locked-stage text is clipped at the card edge in the screenshots.
- Several cards show "0/4" or "0/5 claims checked": falling-yet-adding, few-survivors, five-day-generations, immunity-eats-r, isolate-by-day-three, leaky-vaccine-threshold, pockets-below-threshold, stale-case-counts, waves-return. Launch verdicts on these are contingent on the fact-checker.
- Concrete bugs to route to the builder:
  - antibiotic-already-there: step 2 says "every cell is resistant" while the counter still reads 100.
  - dish-runs-out: the reveal says "2 doubled 30 times is about 1.07 billion", which is wrong.
  - keeping-the-bad-gene: the reveal says 13% after the survival slider has moved the ring to 5%.
  - most-cases-vaccinated: the stage opens at 80% while the question says 90%.

Confidence: moderate. These are simulated-learner criticisms only, not evidence that anyone learns. Next move: the builders, and the evaluation-steward for the demo-crit, to pick up the 11 revise lessons. I did not add board items.

Per lesson (finding → fix):
- **two-ripples-cancel** (FATAL: the reveal said "silent" but silence was never shown, and the last screen had speaker B off) → removed the B toggle. The slider's two QA steps land on the half-wave spot, which is now the milestone. The question now asks which instrument changes. The spring scale is marked in kg for Earth, equal pull arrows hang on both pans, and each world gets its own caption.

- **build-a-balanced-mobile** (last screen had the lump off; "turning" never set up) → "Add lump" comes first in DOM order, so the QA path ends loaded and level at 75 cm. Arm lengths are drawn on the beam, with left/right kg×cm readouts and an arrow for the ruler's own weight. c7 added.
- **clay-boat** (cup naming; 0.56 vs 0.80 L never joined; buoyant push not shown) → shapes renamed so each name is unique, density removed from the question, a push-vs-weight arrow diagram added, and one caption joins the two volumes.
- **coaster-track-shape** ("steep" had no control; formula not explained) → the slider shows slope in degrees, the dashed track is a fixed steep reference, each cart shows its live speed, g and h are defined, and "faster" is reworded. Gated with Milestones. c6 and c7 added; durationSec set to 60.
- **count-the-thunder** (µs; reveal/stage mismatch) → flash time shown in plain seconds, a flash ray is drawn, the caption says "Count ÷ 3 = N km mark", and the reveal uses the learner's own count.
- **crumple-zone-stopping-time** (momentum named before it is defined; no sense of scale) → the stage says mass × speed, force is also given in car-weights, there is a crush-distance readout, the people inside are mentioned, and I applied the fact-check framing fix. c4, c5 and c6 reset; c7 added.
- **current-same-around-loop** (the meter never sat between the bulbs; reveal quoted 6 V) → spot buttons in an order that ends between the bulbs, dots that fade after each bulb (energy) while their count stays the same (current), 2 V battery steps so the bulb shares add up exactly, and a reveal quoting the voltages the learner used. c2 and c5 reset; c7 added.
- **doubling-speed-braking** (energy "because" was only told) → Speed×, Energy× and Road readouts side by side, numbered blocks, and a Milestones gate at 60 km/h. The reaction-time line is removed.
- **dropped-vs-fired-ball** (the reveal never unlocked within the QA wait; no legend) → added a "Jump to landing" step button, a legend, and a clock. The reveal now quotes the runs the learner made. - No separate "now estimate this one" step in count-the-thunder: it needs a new stage state, and the caption check covers the same skill more cheaply.

**Disputed:**
- physics.crumple-zone-stopping-time.c5: "real cars crush less and stop faster than these numbers" doesn't hold against the 0.10 s / 0.75 m case. Published 56 km/h frontal-crash work (NHTSA 18th ESV paper) gives 0.5-0.9 m of crush and pulses around 80-120 ms. It is only true against the 0.20 s case.
- geography.light-in-the-cylinder.c4: "paper touching the globe along one line is true there and stretches everything away from it" is stated generally. It holds only for this light projection; for example, Lambert's cylindrical equal-area compresses north-south distances. Fix: prefix "With a light at the centre,".
- geography.three-giants-in-africa.c6: the hook "On most world maps Africa looks like one big country" has no source. Maps draw its borders, and Mercator makes Africa look smaller. Fix: "On a Mercator map Africa looks smaller than it is", or source and reword it as a claim about what people think.

**Added unverified:** ambulance-pitch-drop.c8 is the stage caption "Each ring is a crest, sent 0.1 s apart". A 700 Hz siren sends crests 1.4 ms apart, so each ring is every 70th crest (the Demo.tsx comment and c5 already say so). I suggested rewording it.

**Skipped or left:**

|---|---|---|---|
| odds-three-to-one | 33% / 25% / 75% → 25% | 5 | pass |
| halved-risk-one-in-thousand | 1 / 10 / 500 → 1 | 5 | pass |
| how-surprising-is-sixty | 0.3% / 3% / 30% → about 3% (exact 2.84%) | 4 | pass |
| second-positive-test | 19% / 50% / 81% → 50% (exact 50.25%) | 5 | pass |
| three-cards-one-red-face | 1/2 / 2/3 / 1/3 → 2/3 | 3 | pass |

**How they are built:**
- Every question and reveal number comes from code in each lesson's `model.ts`, and I re-ran them all in node.
- The reveal stays locked until the key state is reached. The key controls come first in DOM order, so the QA path reaches that state and every value the question and reveal name.

The question asks for heads or tails in a row, which is 0.458 (also 436 of 1,000 in simulation). None of the options (5% / 25% / 75%) is right. I took brief 31, ninety-five-percent-of-what, instead.

- odds-three-to-one uses 4 blocks, not up to 20.

summary: Short version: all three are worth doing, but in a particular order, and two of them need narrowing before we build.
body:
Short version: all three are worth doing, but in a particular order, and two of them need narrowing before we build.

**First, where things stand.** The usage limit hit again and stopped all 8 agents mid-task. Their partial work is safe in their worktrees and I can resume them. We have 318 lessons, 47 of them published.

## 1. Backend team (auth, real app, progress in a database): yes, and it's the most important of the three

Today progress lives only in the browser, so the spaced-recall revisits break if a learner switches device. Worse, we have **zero learning data**: every business review so far has said "no data", because nothing is deployed and no real learners exist. A backend is what turns this from a content factory into a product we can measure.

What I'd build:
- **Deploy first, then add the backend.** The Vercel setup and deploy runbook are ready; I need your account.
- **Anonymous first, sign in later.** Anyone can play without an account. Signing in saves progress and merges the anonymous history into it. Requiring login before the first card would kill the "60-second" feel.
- **Store little data:** the user, each prediction attempt (lesson, choice, correct or not, time) and the revisit schedule. That alone gives us the real recall rate, which is the metric the company is built around.
- **Treat it as a critical change:** a design doc, an architecture decision record for the auth provider and the database, and an engineering review. New dependencies also need decision records under our own rules.

**Decisions I need from you:**
- an auth provider, e.g. Auth.js with email magic links, or Clerk;
- a database host, e.g. Neon or Vercel Postgres;
- **whether learners may be under 13.** That brings in COPPA and GDPR-K, and it changes the design.

## 2. Social and gamification: yes to a small, learning-aligned version; not yet to social

Gamification works for retention (Duolingo, Brilliant), but it easily rewards the wrong thing: points for speed or streaks for opening the app. That's the same Goodhart trap we already caught with QA shaping our lessons.

What I'd do, and when:
- **Gamify recall, not activity.** A "streak" means you did today's revisits, and the mastery map fills in when your recall holds. We already have the map.
- **Hold off on leaderboards and points for now.**
- **Social is heavier than it looks.** It needs moderation, abuse handling and child safety. Start with something light, such as "send this prediction to a friend", and run it as an experiment with predictions committed in advance.
- **Wait for real learners.** Without users we can't tell whether any of this helps.

So: a small growth team, formed after the backend, gated by the analytics steward.

## 3. Company tools team, faster rituals, rooms and a timeline: strongly agree, and it's the cheapest

**Cadence.** You're right that rituals measured in days don't fit agents that work in minutes. I already ran a "mid-cycle" business review because a week was meaningless. I'd make rituals **event-driven**:
- a retro every 50 merged lessons or after any incident;
- a launch review after every publish batch;
- a demo crit every 20 lessons reviewed.

Only the founder-facing ones stay on the calendar, e.g. a daily digest for you.

**Rooms and timeline.** Today the records are markdown and git history, but the actual agent conversations (the reports, my dispatch prompts) aren't kept anywhere you can browse. I'd build:
1. **An append-only event log** in the repo. Every dispatch, report, merge, publish, dispute and incident becomes one line, with links to its records. The disk stays the memory.
2. **An "HQ" page in the app:**
   - a timeline you can scroll back through and filter (per lesson, per agent, per ritual);
   - meeting pages showing the conversation, decisions and objections;
   - Sococo-style rooms (Build floor, Review room, Fact-check desk, Launch room) showing who is working on what right now.

The event log matters more than the rooms picture, so it comes first.

## Recommended order

1. **Company tools** (small, quick): the event log and event-driven rituals, then the HQ timeline and rooms. It helps me run the company and helps you follow it.
2. **Deploy plus backend:** auth, the progress database and server-side events, so real learning metrics start.
3. **Recall-based gamification,** then social, once there are real learners to measure.

Lesson production carries on alongside all of this, but slower. We've hit the usage limit twice, and three new teams compete for the same budget. Do you want me to split the budget, say 50% lessons and 50% new teams, or put lessons on pause until the backend ships?

If this order works for you, I'll set up the three teams (roles, onboarding docs, agents) and start on the event log, and wait for your auth, database and age answers before building the backend.

body:
That helps a lot: a floor plan where you can see at a glance who is where and what they're doing. Here's how I'd map it onto our company, and one thing I'd add that Sococo lacks.

## How it maps

| Sococo | System 3 Company HQ |
|---|---|
| Rooms on a floor plan | One room per team or ritual (layout below) |
| Avatars in rooms | One dot per agent, coloured by role, in the room for its current task |
| Busy / away status | Running, blocked or finished, plus a one-line "now doing…" |
| Room chat | The room's conversation: my dispatch prompt, the agent's report, my decision |
| Meeting rooms | WBR, retro, demo crit, launch review, eng review, COE. Each meeting page has its transcript, decisions and the objections that travel with them |
| Your avatar | You, in the Lobby, with an inbox of "decisions needed from the founder" |

**Floor plan:**
- **Around the edge (team offices):**
  - the 9 category managers
  - Engineering (principal engineer)
  - Backend
  - Growth
  - Company Tools
- **Centre (the work floor):**
  - the Build floor (one desk per domain builder)
  - the Fact-check desk
  - the Learner Review room
  - the QA lab
- **Meeting rooms:**
  - WBR
  - Retro
  - Demo Crit
  - Launch Room
  - Eng Review
  - Incident room (COE)
- **Also:**
  - the Constitution chamber, for amendments
  - the Lobby, which is your office

## What I'd add: a time slider

The feature that matters most for you is "go back and see". Sociocode shows only now. Ours would have a **replay slider**: drag it back to 06:20 and you see the office as it was then, with the right agents at their desks and the conversations they were having. Click a room and you get its timeline. Click a lesson and you get its whole history: built, checked, disputed, fixed, published.

## An honest difference

Agents don't talk to each other live the way people do in Sococo. A "meeting" here is a sequence: I dispatch, the agent works, it reports, I decide. So a room's chat reads like a thread, not a live call.

## How it would work

1. **An event log in the repo** (one append-only file). Every dispatch, report, merge, publish, dispute, incident and ritual becomes one line. The office, the timeline and the replay are all drawn from it, so the disk stays the memory and nothing depends on a separate service.
2. **An `/hq` page in our app:** the floor plan as SVG, with the timeline and the replay slider. It refreshes live while agents run locally, and after deploy it's behind your login.
3. **A Company Tools team** owns it, along with the switch to event-driven rituals.

I'd build it in that order: event log, then the timeline (useful on its own), then the floor plan, then replay.

Should I set up the three teams and start on the event log and HQ now? Also, for the backend: which auth provider and database host do you want, will learners include under-13s, and how should the usage budget be split between new lessons and the new teams? I'll pause the backend until you answer.

body:
The three teams are set up and the first version of HQ works locally. While building it I also merged 10 new chemistry lessons, so we're at 328, and the lesson checks pass with no warnings.

**New teams.** Five new roles, each with an onboarding doc and an agent; the org chart is updated and the reasoning is in a decision record.
- **Backend:** a backend engineer and a privacy & safety reviewer. Play stays anonymous until a learner signs in, and every schema or provider choice gets a design doc and an engineering review. Nothing gets built until you answer the questions below.
- **Growth:** a gamification designer whose rewards point at recall, not taps. Leaderboards for speed or volume are ruled out, and every feature runs as an experiment.
- **Company Tools:** a tools lead and an HQ engineer, who own the event log, HQ and the ritual triggers.

**What HQ does.** It opens at `/hq` on a local server; it's off in production for now because it shows internal agent briefs and reports.
- **Floor plan:** offices, meeting rooms and the work floor, with each agent shown as a dot in the room of its current task. The 8 agents stopped by the usage limit show in their rooms with a red ring.
- **Replay:** drag the slider, press Replay to watch the day, or click the coloured event strip. Any moment can be linked, e.g. `/hq?t=2026-10-13T06:20Z&room=build-floor`.
- **Room threads:** each room's history in order (my dispatch briefs, the agents' reports, decisions); click an event to read it in full.
- **Lobby (your office):** rituals due now, the board items waiting on you, and our conversation.
- **Event log:** HQ reads from `company/ops/events.jsonl`. It's already filled with about 590 events from git history and this session, including all 94 agents and your messages, and it refreshes on every commit.

**Rituals run on events now.** A retro fires every 5 merged batches or after any incident, a demo crit every 4 review batches, and a launch review after every review or fact-check batch. You also get a digest at least every 12 hours. `node tools/rituals-due.mjs` lists what's due, and HQ shows it. Right now that's the retro, the demo crit, a launch review and your first digest.

**Running again.** The usage limit stopped all 8 agents for about 7 hours. I've resumed the AI and geography builders, the life sciences reviser and three reviewers (economics, computer science, geography).

**Questions for you:**
1. Which auth provider and which database host for the backend?
2. Will learners include children under 13?
3. How should the usage budget be split between new lessons and the three new teams?

body:
I built the next 10 ai briefs in order (31–40). All 10 pass computer-use QA on phone and desktop, and check, tsc and next build are clean. Nothing was skipped and nothing is pushed.

Branch `worktree-agent-a384906e06bef5dca`, 5 commits: c340763, 3fa1bf7, 9ccc9f2, 59b3870, 61b1b29. Each commits 2 lessons with the registry. The last commit's subject names only its 2 slugs; its body carries the full "Wave 4 ai: <all 10 slugs>" line and the Co-Authored-By line.

| slug | prediction → answer | claims | QA |
|---|---|---|---|
| word-in-pieces | 11 / 3 / 1 tokens → 3 | 5 | pass |
| outlier-flattens-line | 0.8 / 0.5 / exactly 0 → 0 | 4 | pass |
| one-nudge-per-mistake | 1 / 2 / 5 nudges → 2 | 4 | pass |
| duplicates-in-the-test | 50 / 60 / 80% → 60% | 4 | pass |
| five-weak-voters | 60 / ~68 / ~90% → 68.3% | 5 | pass |
| shrink-toward-zero | A / B / equal → B (0.125 vs 0.25) | 4 | pass |
| stop-at-epoch-sixty | end / before step 100 / step 0 → before 100 | 4 | pass |
| confident-and-wrong | 1.4 / 4.6 / 50 → 4.6 | 4 | pass |
| say-seventy-mean-it | 90 / 70 / 50% → 70% | 4 | pass |
| greedy-word-trap | greedy / other / tie → other (36 vs 24%) | 4 | pass |

All claims are "unverified" and every lesson is status "review" with builder "demo-builder". Each lesson has a build note at `company/reviews/<slug>/build.md`. Every number was recomputed in node, and the question and reveal numbers come from the same code that draws the stage. Each reveal is gated by 1–2 milestones that the QA path reaches, and answer readouts are hidden until the prediction is locked.

Where I departed from the briefs (all recorded in the build notes):
- **stop-at-epoch-sixty:** I built my own toy instead of the brief's LCG. It uses seed 12, which I chose to show a clear dip; the stage says "(chosen)" and the question says "In this run". The reveal gives the spread: in 483 of 500 seeds the lowest held-out error comes before the end of training. Only 123 of 500 seeds have it before step 100, so that option is true of this run, not in general.
- **duplicates-in-the-test:** "guesses 50/50 on new items" became "always says yes; half the true answers are yes", so the fresh-item score is exactly 50%.
- **say-seventy-mean-it:** the model is right on exactly 14 of 20, so the stage's average matches the formula with no seed luck.
- **shrink-toward-zero:** the best shrink factor is exactly 0.5, not "~0.6" as the brief says.
- **outlier-flattens-line:** the fifth point starts at (5,5), so the slope 1 in the question is what the stage shows first.

One trap worth sharing: QA counts the stage controls once, before it presses anything. greedy-word-trap first failed because its second-word buttons appeared only after a first word was picked, so QA never reached them. That row now always renders 3 slots.

My confidence is high on the arithmetic and the gates, medium on teaching quality, which no evaluator or learner has tested yet.

Next: the fact-checker should verify the 42 claims, starting with the seed-dependent ones in stop-at-epoch-sixty (c1, c2) and five-weak-voters (c2). Evaluators then run walkthroughs. I did not update `company/ops/board.json` or `company/ops/progress.md`, since the brief put those out of scope; the caller or chief of staff owns them. The untracked `test-results-w4ai/` folder is QA output and was left out of the commits.

- antibiotic-already-there: step 2 said "every cell is resistant" next to a counter of 100 → it now says the survivors regrow and every cell descends from a resistant one, and the readout shows "all". The 0.1 at 10 million was never shown → the readout now shows expected counts for every dish size, with a new "small-dish" milestone. "Resistance mutation" is defined in the question.

"Dish full" is stated at 10 h, and "stopped" became "levelled off".
- hidden-carriers: "squared" was told but not shown → the stage shows the copy share (1 in 100, 100 × 100 = 10,000) at every setting. "1 in 51" is now "about 1 in 50". The "Carriers each" label is now "Carriers per person showing it". The reveal's 18 comes from a milestone that requires 1 in 100. The hook no longer leaks.
- keeping-the-bad-gene: I replaced the ring with a trace of both starts (1% and 50%) rising and falling to a dashed "balance" line. The reveal said 13% after the learner's slider moved to 5% → it now quotes 13% for the default and adds a computed sentence for the learner's own slider setting. The option no longer names 13%, and "allele" is glossed.
- most-cases-vaccinated: the stage opened at 80% but the question said 90% → it opens at 90%. A 0/50/90/100% chip row replaces the slider, and milestones for 0% and 100% gate the reveal. The title and hook no longer give the answer, and the question now says "cuts that to 5%" so the arithmetic is easy.
- one-in-four-sprouts: the reveal's 42% contradicted the 49 on the stage → it quotes the learner's own 100-family counts and says another field would differ. P/w is explained before the first family. The title and hook no longer leak.
- pesticide-paradox: break-even was told, not shown → the question states the mechanism, and a dashed predator average sits beside the pest average. The reveal quotes the strength the learner set. The chart label overlap is fixed, and the title and hook no longer leak. I removed the Volterra aside and marked claim c4 "withdrawn" rather than leaving it unshown.
- saturated-enzyme: 91 and 50 were never shown → every setting now shows its own "from" state (busy 91 → 95), with newly busy stations in a second colour. The question is split into short sentences. "Versus half as much" and the formula are gone, the two percentage tiles are relabelled, and the hook no longer leans "no".
- spreaders-are-rare: "negative binomial, dispersion k" and the k button labels are replaced by plain words (Even / Uneven / Very uneven). The largest circle is now labelled, so the "7" is visible. The reveal notes the totals are rounded (199 to 201). The told-only "chains die out" sentence is removed.
- strategy-builder: the 5%/7% buttons bracketed the answer → a 1–30% start slider plus a "Start at 25%, run" button, with the four pairing scores and both running averages in a table. The told equation is removed, the reveal quotes the learner's own losing and winning starts, and the "cheat 14.0 with no cheats" display is fixed. From 6% the share grows but is only 18 of 100 at generation 60, so the test is "grew vs shrank", not "took over".
- waves-return: waves were never shown → a chart of the susceptible (grey) and sick (red) shares against the dashed 50% line. The reveal's 50.0% disagreed with the stage's 50.7% → it now quotes the stage's number. There is a new "other immunity length" milestone. Not fixed: the "0/5 claims checked" badge in waves-return is verification state, not a defect, so I left it to the fact-checker.

Reviewed all 30 cs lessons that lacked a learner review (the 25 first, then the 5 you released: the-contrary-program, tournament-second-best, two-flips-slip-by, wave-from-the-corner, wheel-of-negatives). No lessons left unreviewed, no 404s (the only "404" hit was digits in 0.30000000000000004 in pennies-dont-add-up). Boundary: adult who uses a phone and laptop, never programmed. Section 1 was written before I opened meta.json. Image reads worked first time after the early batches' placeholders; I re-read those and none failed. Where a folder held stale screenshots from an old run, I used the fresh reveal file.

Files: /home/user/system-3-company/company/reviews/<slug>/2026-10-13-learner-adult-beginner.md for each of the 30. I edited nothing else and did not commit. The walkthrough transcripts and screenshots are under /home/user/system-3-company/artifacts/walkthroughs/.

Verdicts: launch 8, revise 21, fatal 1.
- Launch: call-stack-depth, lopsided-tree, lru-eviction-order, pivot-lands-home, quadratic-wall, runs-that-grow, sketch-the-counts, tournament-second-best.
- Revise: back-button-stack, bad-hash-one-bucket, big-number-swallows-one, bisect-the-bad-commit, coin-greedy-trap, fib-call-explosion, flip-and-add-one, half-adder-wiring, hanoi-tower-doubles, hash-bucket-pileup, heap-bubble-up, insertion-by-hand, list-doubling-copies, maze-depth-first, one-bit-avalanche, pennies-dont-add-up, route-explosion, the-contrary-program, two-flips-slip-by, wave-from-the-corner, wheel-of-negatives.
- Fatal: huffman-by-merging. The reveal says the 14-bit total, then lists "A 00, B 01, C 11, D 10" as the codes. That is the four 2-bit codes, which cost 16, so the reveal contradicts its own 14. The default tap path also never shows the 14-bit tree. The fix is small.

Three most common findings:
1. The reveal's key payoff is told, not shown. Examples: the fib(30) count, the 9-vs-13 matches in tournament-second-best, the bigger maze in maze-depth-first, and the 24- and 120-route cases in route-explosion. The stage path or auto-run buttons skip the steps the reveal quotes.
2. The hook or question gives the answer away or names jargon the stage never defines. Hooks leaking: bisect-the-bad-commit, insertion-by-hand, pennies-dont-add-up. Jargon: mod, hash, min-heap, two's complement, parity, SHA-256.
3. The stage on screen at the reveal does not match the reveal text. Examples: Reset or Restart left an empty stage, the half-adder circuit was gone, and in two-flips-slip-by only adjacent flips were tried while the reveal says "wherever they are". Reveal text is also clipped at the card bottom in many screenshots.

Other notes:
- lru-eviction-order: the reveal claims LRU "keeps more hits", but the stage showed identical hits and misses under both rules.
- big-number-swallows-one: the trust sheet I could see lists one claim as DISPUTED, and that sentence is in the reveal.
- Confidence: moderate. These are simulated-learner criticisms and hypotheses, not evidence that anyone learned.
- Next move: each lesson's builder (or category manager) reads its review and revises. Huffman is the urgent one. Evaluation-steward can schedule human-learner checks for the 8 launch verdicts.

  - ai.stop-at-epoch-sixty c1 and c2 hold. Seed 12 gives held-out error 0.751, 0.299 (step 67), 0.320, 0.486 and 0.693. The lowest error comes before the end in 483 of 500 seeds, and the stage labels the seed as chosen.

My estimate is about 3.4 °C: the ideal 3.72 °C times the osmotic coefficient gives 3.4 to 3.46 °C, and measured data for 5.5% NaCl interpolate to about 3.4 °C. I could not open the CRC table, so I did not dispute it. The builder owns the fix: change the stage's muted line and the claim to "about 3.4 °C".
  - geography.half-of-humanity.c1: population.un.org is still unreachable. Only aggregators confirm the figures, so I left it unverified as you instructed.

  - geography.three-giants-in-africa.c6: "Africa looks smaller than it is" is true only relative to the US and China. Suggested hook: "…next to the US and China."
  - chemistry.which-dissolves-in-oil.c3: calling sucrose "charged ends" is loose but acceptable.

# Retro: 2026-10-13 (evening): 298 → 348 lessons, HQ, new teams

owner: chief-of-staff · input: 14 agent reports since the 06:40 retro, the event log, the launch-review record

## Numbers
- **Lessons:** 50 added (geography w3 and w4, probability w3, chemistry w4, ai w4) and about 60 revised (physics, probability, life, the fatals, claim fixes). 0 merge QA failures.
- **Fact-checks:** passes 4 and 5 covered 80 lessons: 3 disputed, all fixed the same evening. Claims are 96% verified.
- **Learner reviews:** 145 lessons reviewed. Current verdicts: 64 launch, 81 revise, 0 fatal; 52 are stale after revision.
- **Published:** 56.
- **Usage-limit stops:** 2 more (3 today), each stopping every running agent for hours.

## What went well
- **Revisions are cheap and they work.** A Sonnet reviser fixed 11 life lessons for about 20k tokens each. The fatals were fixed within an hour of being found.
- **The holds file caught 3 cases** the gate would have shipped: lru-eviction-order, which a sentence on its own stage contradicts; friends-have-more-friends, which has a false verified claim; and 8 launches written without screenshots.
- **The event log made HQ possible** with no new process: the snapshot backfills it.

## What hurt (with evidence)
1. **Usage limit (3 times today).** The biggest throughput loss of the day: about 7 h and then about 1 h with nothing running.
2. **Evidence quality varies by reviewer.** The geography reviewer's image reads failed for 21 lessons and verdicts were written anyway. One launch (eratosthenes-shadow) was published on that basis and then unpublished. Mitigation already in the brief: no "launch" without screenshots seen.
3. **Two publishes went wrong, both by me.** friends-have-more-friends went out because a hold was lifted in the same command as a merge that failed. eratosthenes-shadow was published before the reviewer reported its caveat. Both were reverted within minutes.
4. **`pgrep -f`/`pkill -f` killed my own shell again,** despite the checklist rule. The rule existed but wasn't followed, so it needs a mechanism.
5. **A resumed builder found its worktree deleted.** I clean worktrees only for finished agents, but a stopped agent's worktree with no commits can still disappear. No work was lost.

## What we will change
| Change | Mechanism | Owner | Board id |
|---|---|---|---|
| Publish only after every running review batch has reported | publish loop runs on report events only, never mid-batch | chief-of-staff | — |
| No process killing by pattern | `tools/serve.sh start/stop <port>` with pid files; the checklist points at it | tools-lead | W-072 |
| Budget-aware dispatch | at most 6 agents; before a dispatch wave, check the time since the last limit hit; long reviews split into batches of ≤15 lessons so a stop loses less | chief-of-staff | — |
| Reviews say whether screenshots were seen | learner-review format gains `screenshots: seen/not seen`; publish-ready refuses "not seen" | evaluation-steward (proposal), tools-lead | W-073 |

## What we will stop doing
- Starting more than 3 builders and 3 reviewers at once while the budget is unknown.

## Did last retro's changes work?
- **Review capacity ≥ build capacity:** partly. Reviews went from 89 to 145, but builds and revisions created 52 stale reviews.
- **Integrated QA after each merge batch:** yes. A stale build was caught by the new freshness check.
- **The publish-loop tool:** yes, with the holds file it is now the only publish path.

body:
Not the way we build lessons today. 1M is reachable, but only by changing what a lesson is. Here's the math and what I'd change.

**What breaks at 1M**

| Today, per lesson | × 1M |
|---|---|
| About 35–50k tokens to build, fact-check, review and revise it | About 50 billion tokens |
| A builder writes custom code for each lesson | 1M lesson folders in git, 1M pages in every build |
| About 5 claims checked one by one | 5M claim checks |
| A browser QA run per lesson (2 screen sizes) | About 11,000 hours of QA per full run |
| 3–8 agents in parallel, which hit the usage limit three times today | Decades at this pace |

They hit it again an hour ago: all 6 agents are stopped until about 22:10 UTC. Their partial work is committed, and I'll resume them after the reset.

**The shifts that make it possible**

1. **Lessons become data.** Instead of a new Demo.tsx each time, we build about 300–500 reusable interaction types. Examples: "slide a parameter and watch a curve", "simulate N trials", "a projection explorer", "a balance". A lesson becomes a short data file: the question, the parameters, the values the learner must reach, the reveal text. Writing one costs a few thousand tokens on a small model instead of about 20k on Opus. The lesson checks everything mechanically: whether the named values are reachable, whether the answer readout is hidden, how long the reveal is.
2. **Numbers check themselves.** Most claims are computed by the engine, so verifying an engine once covers every lesson built on it. Facts from outside sources go into a shared fact library: "Greenland is 2.17 million km²" is checked once and reused by every lesson that needs it.
3. **Variants multiply the concepts.** There probably aren't 1M distinct things worth teaching; Brilliant has a few thousand lessons. 1M is more like 10k concepts × 4 levels × 25 languages, plus variants in different everyday contexts (sports, cooking, money).
4. **Build on demand.** Don't pre-build 1M. Pre-build the core of about 10k, generate a variant the first time a learner needs it, cache it, and keep it only if its numbers hold up.
5. **Check samples, not everything.** Each batch gets a random sample of 2–5% fully reviewed, and the batch ships only if the defect rate is low enough. Health, money and anything aimed at children keep a full check on every lesson.
6. **Real learners become the judge.** Simulated reviewers stay for new interaction types and for samples. The deciding signal becomes real recall data per lesson, and the weakest lessons are retired or revised automatically. That needs the backend we discussed, so the backend becomes the critical path.
7. **Infrastructure:**
   - Content moves from git to a database plus file storage with version history; git keeps only the code.
   - Pages render from data at request time behind a CDN, instead of a build of 1M pages.
   - QA tests each interaction type once, plus automated tests that feed it random lesson data.
   - The event log moves to a real database.
   - Generation runs through the API's batch mode with organisation-level rate limits, not interactive sessions.
8. **The org changes shape:**
   - Builders become engine engineers.
   - Category managers become curriculum-graph editors.
   - Most content is written by small, cheap models, with Opus spot-reviewing.
   - HQ shows each team's dashboards rather than one dot per agent.

**Milestones**

| Step | What it proves |
|---|---|
| 1k (where we are) | Hand-built lessons, learning what makes one good |
| 10k | Interaction types plus data files, sampled QA, deployed, real recall data |
| 100k | Levels, languages, the fact library, automatic retirement |
| 1M | Variants generated on demand and kept only if learners' recall holds up |

**The honest risk is quality, not volume.** Today only about 45% of lessons pass learner review the first time, even with careful builders. Generating a million copies of a 55% defect rate is a million bad lessons. The quality loop has to be measured on real learners before it's worth multiplying.

**My recommendation:** finish the push to 500 hand-built lessons, then deploy and get real learners on them. Next, extract the 20–30 interaction types the existing lessons already repeat. Then test the data-file approach on one domain: geography maps or probability simulations are the natural first candidates. If you'd like, I'll have Kenji, our principal engineer, write it up as a design doc (EDD-003, "Scaling to 1M"), with cost estimates using current model prices.

summary: I've added your direction to Kenji's design doc. It now treats "every lesson compiled into one app" as ruled out at scale. The main questio…
body:
I've added your direction to Kenji's design doc. It now treats "every lesson compiled into one app" as ruled out at scale. The main question is where lesson code loads at runtime: on the server, in the browser, or a mix.

My view, as a starting point for Kenji's review rather than a decision: **load lesson code in the browser, not on the server.**

- **Lessons don't need a server.** Each one is a self-contained interactive card: predict, explore, reveal. All the computing already happens on the learner's phone, so running lesson code on a server would add load without adding anything.
- **Running generated code on a server is the riskiest place to run it.** A bad lesson on the server could reach other users' data and the database. In the browser it can be boxed in: each lesson runs in a sandboxed frame on a separate domain and can only send "predicted / revealed / recall" messages to the app. It can never see sign-in tokens.
- **The server becomes tiny.** It only serves a lesson index: which lessons exist, the current version of each, and their text and claims. Lesson code sits on a CDN as unchangeable files named by their content hash, so cost per view is close to zero and nothing is compiled when a lesson is added.
- **It fits how we work.** Each lesson version is built and QA'd once, then never changes. Rolling back means pointing the index at the previous file, and every version stays addressable for the review records.
- **What has to be designed carefully:**
  - how independently built lessons share one versioned copy of the kit;
  - loading the next 2 cards ahead in the feed so swipes stay instant;
  - previews for search engines;
  - offline play.

I've asked Kenji to compare all three options on these points. I also asked him for a small experiment before any migration: load 3 existing lessons as separate runtime files and see what breaks. If the usage limit stops him, I'll resume him after the reset around 22:10 UTC, and you'll get his recommendation, the review record and his questions for you.

summary: PE: EDD-003 lesson storage at scale: I wrote EDD-003 and opened the engineering review. My recommendation: lesson code loads in the browser, never…
body:
I wrote EDD-003 and opened the engineering review. My recommendation: lesson code loads in the browser, never on the server. The server sends only a list of lessons, their metadata and preview images. Each lesson is built on its own into a code file named by its hash, stored on a CDN, and run in a locked-down iframe on a separate domain. No code, gates or protected paths were changed, nothing was committed, and `npm run check` passes.

**Baseline at 348 lessons (measured):**
- **Repo:** 6.8 files per lesson (3.1 source, 3.7 review records), about 17 KB per lesson. Git history is 4.26 MB packed over 278 commits; `git status` takes 0.016 s and `check` 0.57 s.
- **Build:** 73 s (25 s compile, 26 s type check, 10.5 s rendering 353 pages). Output is 321 MB, of which 196 MB is server output, about 0.56 MB per lesson. The registry file is 53 KB.
- **QA:** 12.2 s of browser time per lesson across the two screen sizes, 6.6 s of wall time per lesson with 2 workers. A fresh sample of 18 lessons took 118 s.

**Two budgets are already broken today:**
- The feed page is 1.82 MB against EDD-001's 300 KB budget, so EDD-001's trigger has already fired.
- A 1.29 MB file (349 KB compressed) holding every lesson's full metadata, claims included, loads on the feed and on every lesson page.
- Smaller finding: the map code and data used by geography lessons is copied into 3 separate files of about 1.45 MB each.

**Where it breaks (linear extrapolation, medium confidence):**
- The single app build, the registry and full-catalog QA break between 2k and 10k lessons. At 10k that means about 35 min per build, 5.6 GB of output, 18 h of QA and a 37 MB metadata file.
- Plain git with full checkouts breaks near 100k (680k files, about 2.5 GB of history).
- At 1M, a full QA run would take about 3,400 browser-hours.
- The launch gate needs every review record to exist as a local file, so a partial checkout would break it.

**On the founder's server-or-client question:**
- Loading lessons on the server is rejected. Agent-written code would run in the process that will hold credentials, every lesson view costs a server call, and we gain nothing because lessons already render only in the browser.
- The fallback is loading lessons directly into the page without an iframe. That is acceptable only until learner login exists.
- The shared lesson kit gets version numbers, and each lesson records which version it was built against. A lesson's version is its slug plus a hash, and every claim check and review record cites that hash. QA runs once per lesson version. Rollback means pointing the lesson list back at the previous hash.
- Levels, languages and contexts become data applied to one lesson's code, not copied folders.

**Stages:**
- **Now to 1k:** fix EDD-001 (slim feed index, pagination, split registry), add lesson version hashes, and run a spike first: load why-seven-wins, throw-it-fast-enough and bearing-spiral-to-the-pole as separate files in iframes. Budgets: 15 KB compressed or less per lesson, card usable within 300 ms after scrolling to it, and a negative test that lesson code cannot reach the host's cookies or storage.
- **1k to 10k:** separately built lessons on the CDN and a generated lesson list. Start at 1k lessons, a build over 10 min or full QA over 2 h.
- **10k to 100k:** lesson sources move into repos split by domain, still in git. Start when the repo passes 1 GB, `git status` takes over 1 s, a fresh checkout takes over 60 s, or at 20k lessons.
- **Beyond 100k:** decide then, with data.
- Every stage can be reversed except the last.

**What I would not do yet:** load code on the server, move off git, use Postgres or submodules, rewrite the existing lessons onto a shared engine, add new dependencies, or change what any gate demands.

**Proposed ADRs:**
- ADR-003: lesson code never runs on the server.
- ADR-004: each lesson version is immutable and named by its hash.
- ADR-005: lessons are built separately against a versioned kit.
- ADR-006: lessons run in a locked-down iframe on a separate domain.
- ADR-007: the lesson list replaces the registry, and rollback is a pointer change.
- ADR-008: variants are data, not code.
- ADR-009 (stage 2): domain-split content repos.
- Plus a decision record on which build tool to use.
- The gate changes (registry, QA tied to the lesson hash, index-based lookups) need amendments drafted by the evaluation steward.

**Founder questions:**
1. Is 1M really 1M distinct interactions, or concepts times variants?
2. Does a translation need its claims checked again?
3. When does login arrive?
4. How much does SEO matter?
5. Is offline play required?
6. Is the budget for CDN and CI browser time acceptable?
7. Does "the disk is the memory" mean git specifically?

body:
Yes, but there's a catch: the bottleneck is the usage limit, not the number of agents. Today we hit the limit three times while running only 6–8 agents, and every hit stopped all of them for between half an hour and seven hours. More agents in parallel spend the same budget faster, so we hit the next stop sooner without getting more lessons per day. Disk and memory in this container aren't the bottleneck; they could handle 10 or so.

So the useful kind of "more parallel" is more agents per unit of budget:

1. **Cheaper models for more roles.** The Sonnet revisers did good work today: 11 life lessons at about 20k tokens each. I'll test Sonnet for new lessons too, in two domains alongside the Opus builders, and compare launch rates before switching more over.
2. **Smaller briefs.** Builders currently read about 10 files before they start. A compact build brief could cut roughly a quarter of their tokens.
3. **More budget.** If you can raise the plan's usage limit, I can safely go to 10–12 agents.

I'm adding three Sonnet agents now: builders for the next 10 economics and next 10 chemistry lessons, and a fact-checker for the 40 newest lessons. That makes 8 running, with Opus still capped at 3 builders.

summary: Only partly. Category managers today own their own curriculum map, the order of their briefs and coverage within their category. Nothing ma…
body:
Only partly. Category managers today own their own curriculum map, the order of their briefs and coverage within their category. Nothing makes anyone check that a lesson adds something distinct, or that it doesn't repeat another category's lesson. Their onboarding docs never mention overlap or portfolio value. And the push to 500 rewarded volume: I wrote round 2 of the briefs to fill about 55 per domain.

**What I found in a quick scan of all 368 lessons:**
- **Same idea in two categories:**
  - the Sieve of Eratosthenes, in CS (sieve-stops-at-five) and math (sieve-crossing-out);
  - Euclid's algorithm, in CS (euclid-leftover-rectangle) and math (euclid-square-cutting);
  - the rule of 72, in economics (rule-of-72-shortcut) and math (seventy-two-doubling).
- **14 concepts with two lessons each:** for example two's complement, hash collisions, recursion, vaccine thresholds and genetic inheritance. Some are deliberate second angles, which can help learners when it's intentional. Others look like the same lesson twice.
- **Themes spread across categories with no owner:** exponential growth appears in math, economics, life sciences and chemistry, and nobody decides which lesson is the main one and which are transfer lessons that apply it in a new setting.

**What I'd add:**
1. **One distinct insight per lesson,** stated in every brief: the misconception it overturns, plus its nearest existing lessons and why it's different. The category manager approves that before anything gets built.
2. **An overlap check:** a tool that flags similar lessons, including across categories, whenever a brief or lesson is added. It warns rather than blocks, since the publish gates are constitutional.
3. **A portfolio review ritual,** triggered every 20 lessons in a category. Each manager looks at:
   - value: demand, coverage gaps and real-learner recall once we have it;
   - redundancy: which lessons to merge, retire or relabel as deliberate practice;
   - what's missing.
4. **A shared owner for each cross-category theme** (growth, algorithms, probability in life sciences). They choose one main lesson, and the others must be labelled transfer lessons.

**Two decisions for you:**
- Should the 500 count only distinct lessons, so that near-duplicates don't count until they're merged or turned into deliberate transfer lessons? I'd recommend yes.
- Should I build the overlap check and run a first cross-category portfolio review now? It needs one reviewer agent, which fits within today's budget.

body:
**Verdict: go with changes for EDD-003 stage 1.** The sandboxed iframe works for all 3 lessons in Chromium. Two changes block stage 1: lessons need their own registrable domain with CSP sent as an HTTP header, and the spike has to be re-run on real iOS Safari and Android Chrome. Committed on my branch as 38191e3, not pushed.

**Numbers vs budgets** (Pixel 7 emulation, median of 7 runs; the machine was shared with other agents at load ~30, so times run high):
- **Lesson bundles (≤15 KB gzip):** pass. why-seven-wins 2,502 B, throw-it-fast-enough 2,327 B, bearing-spiral-to-the-pole 2,237 B. All 348 lessons build through the same pipeline: max 8.3 KB, none over 15 KB, none imports anything outside the kit contract.
- **Shared kit (≤120 KB gzip):** pass. React + kit is 61.8 KB. The geo kit is a separate 71 KB that only the 35 geo lessons load, once; today it is duplicated in 3 chunks of about 420 KB.
- **Cold load (≤1.5 s):** pass. Iframe insert to interactive is 190–356 ms, and 0.6–1.1 s with the CPU slowed 4× to mimic a mid phone.
- **Warm load (≤300 ms):** not met as I measured it. Reloading a frame from cache takes 0.2–0.7 s, because every frame starts React again. The feed pre-creates the next frames, and those are ready before the swipe lands, but I did not put a number on "interactive after the swipe". I suggest redefining this budget and measuring it on a device.
- **Memory (≤1.5× today):** pass at 0.85×. Today's feed with 3 cards is 386 MB, the spike with 3 frames 327 MB.

**Security test:** passes on phone and desktop. A control first shows host-page code can read the planted cookie, storage and page text. Then all 19 attempts from a hostile lesson-shaped bundle are blocked: cookies, storage, IndexedDB, host and sibling page content, navigating the top window, popups, form posts, fetch/beacon/image calls to the host, and forged progress or events for another lesson. The host checked its own side too: its server never received a request from a frame. Two findings change the design:
- The sandbox alone does not stop requests out of the frame; the CSP does. So the CDN must send the CSP as a header, not only the meta tag.
- On localhost cookies ignore ports, so the host's session cookie reached the CDN with each frame-document request (frame code still could not read it).

**QA through the iframe:** works. A copy of the contract in `spike/qa/` passes 6/6 (3 lessons × 2 viewports) with locator changes only. Making it the real contract is an amendment for the evaluation steward.

**What broke or needed a change:**
- Progress would be silently lost in the frame (no localStorage there). The build swaps in a bridge module so progress goes to the host; `Lesson.tsx` is unchanged.
- `globals.css` blocks swipes inside a frame (`overscroll-behavior: none`) and mixes app and lesson styles; it should be split.
- `dvh` units mean the frame's height inside a frame.
- Chrome pauses animation frames in off-screen frames, so the ready signal can't rely on them.
- The feed's j/k keys don't work while focus is in a frame.
- The geo kit carries an atlas (`land-110m`) the geography lesson doesn't use.
- No problems with CSS modules, fonts or theme colour. Swiping from inside a frame and dragging sliders work in emulation.

**Rollback:** the manifest went A → B → A, each repoint 1–12 ms, with no rebuild. A fresh load got exactly the pointed bundle each time, and the bundles stayed byte-identical.

**Dependencies:** none added, so no decision record. The spike uses copies of webpack and terser that ship inside Next, plus TypeScript and postcss. Those copies are not a public API, so stage 1 needs a bundler decision record (W-080).

**Checks:** `npx tsc --noEmit`, `NEXT_DIST_DIR=.next-spike npx next build` and `company check` all pass; `tsconfig.json` restored.

**Next moves:** I put four follow-ups on the board:
- W-077, real-device run: me.
- W-078, separate lesson domain and CSP header: privacy-reviewer.
- W-079, the QA amendment: evaluation-steward.
- W-080, bundler decision record: me.

W-074 is in review. The principal engineer closes the review, where I've added my findings.

- `company/engineering/spikes/SPIKE-001-frontend-sandbox.md` (full write-up and how to reproduce)
- `company/engineering/spikes/SPIKE-001-results.json`

summary: The sandbox spike is done. Noor's verdict on stage 1 of the design is go with changes: the approach works, with two things to fix before it…
body:
The sandbox spike is done. Noor's verdict on stage 1 of the design is go with changes: the approach works, with two things to fix before it goes further.

| Budget | Result |
|---|---|
| Lesson file ≤ 15 KB compressed | Passes: the three spike lessons are about 2.3–2.5 KB. All 348 existing lessons were built the same way; the largest is 8.3 KB. |
| Shared kit ≤ 120 KB | Passes at 62 KB. The map code is a separate 71 KB, loaded only by geography lessons. |
| Cold load to interactive ≤ 1.5 s | Passes: 0.2–0.4 s, or 0.6–1.1 s on a simulated mid-range phone. |
| Warm load ≤ 300 ms | Not met as measured: 0.2–0.7 s when reopening a cached frame. The feed prepares the next cards ahead, which should hide this, but it needs measuring on a real phone. |
| Memory | Better than today: 0.85×. |
| Security | All 19 attacks from a hostile test lesson were blocked: reading cookies, storage or the page; navigating away; popups; requests back to the app; faking another lesson's progress. |
| Rollback | Switching a lesson version back and forth took 1–12 ms, with no rebuild. |
| QA through the frame | Our QA checks pass with selector changes only. Making that official is a constitutional amendment. |

**Changes needed before stage 1:**
1. **A separate lesson domain, with security rules sent by the server.** The sandbox alone doesn't stop a lesson from making network requests out of its frame; the content-security policy does. So the CDN must send that policy as a server header, on a domain of its own.
2. **A re-run on a real iPhone and Android phone.** Everything so far ran in emulation on a busy machine.

**Smaller fixes it found:**
- **Progress:** it would have been silently lost inside the frame. It's now relayed to the app, with no change to the lesson kit.
- **Styles:** the app's styles blocked swiping inside a frame and need splitting.
- **Map data:** the map code carries data the geography lessons don't use.

No new packages were added. The spike borrowed bundler copies that ship inside Next, so stage 1 needs a decision record on which bundler to use. The four follow-ups are on the board (W-085 to W-088). The design-doc review stays open for Kenji to close with these results, then it comes to you.

You are a Demo Builder at System 3 Company (worktree = your cwd). Read company/roles/demo-builder.md, company/product/demo-standard.md (QA counts stage controls once BEFORE pressing, then presses each of the first 16 once in DOM order, ~450 ms wait — controls must exist from the start; a button that changes nothing fails QA), src/kit/Lesson.tsx, src/kit/controls.tsx, src/kit/milestones.tsx, src/kit/random.ts, company/knowledge/patterns/{earn-the-reveal,numbers-from-the-stage,disclose-chosen-seeds,label-the-model-on-the-stage}.md, and exemplars src/demos/life/selfing-halves-hets/ and src/demos/probability/cards-do-remember/.
SETUP: `cp -al /home/user/system-3-company/node_modules node_modules`.
GETTING WORK — use the shared queue (other builders are working forward through the same lists): before each lesson run `node /home/user/system-3-company/tools/claim.mjs next life --from-end --agent="queue-builder-1"`; when it prints NONE, switch to `… next probability --from-end …`; stop after 8 lessons in total or when both print NONE. Build exactly the slug it prints (find its brief in company/domains/briefs/<domain>.md). If a brief is wrong/unbuildable, run `node /home/user/system-3-company/tools/claim.mjs release <slug>`, say why in your report, and claim the next.
RULES (non-negotiable): commit after EVERY 2 finished lessons; look at the phone screenshot of EVERY lesson and fix what you see; re-compute every number in node; question numbers from the same code the stage draws, and the QA path MUST visit every value the question and reveal name; state model assumptions on the stage; gate the reveal with <Milestones>, reachable on the QA path; hide answer readouts while locked; reveal ≤ 90 words quoting only what the learner reached (random runs: quote the learner's own run); every learner-visible fact is a claim (`<domain>.<slug>.cN`, "unverified"); seeds via mulberry32, disclosed; retitle titles that give the answer away; CSS modules; ≤25 words stage text.
PER LESSON: `node tools/company.mjs new-demo <domain> <slug>` → meta.json (status "review", builder "demo-builder") → Demo.tsx → company/reviews/<slug>/build.md (note: sonnet build, EXP-003, queue).
VERIFY until green: registry + check (0 errors); `npx tsc --noEmit`; `NEXT_DIST_DIR=.next-q1 npx next build`; `NEXT_DIST_DIR=.next-q1 QA_PORT=3693 QA_OUT=test-results-q1 QA_ONLY=<slugs> npx playwright test tests/qa/contract.spec.ts --workers=2` (pick another 36xx on 404s); `git checkout tsconfig.json`.
DO NOT edit kit/app/components/tests/tools/content/company/ops/company/domains or other domains.
FINISH: final commit "Queue build: <slugs>" + "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>". Do not push. Report ≤25 lines incl. screenshots looked at.

summary: Done: there's now a lock-file work queue, `tools/claim.mjs`.
body:
Done: there's now a lock-file work queue, `tools/claim.mjs`.

- **How a builder gets work:** it runs `claim.mjs next <domain> --agent=<name>` and receives the next unbuilt brief with an exclusive lock. If two builders ask at the same instant, exactly one gets each brief. I ran that race on purpose and they got different briefs.
- **Locks are shared** in the main checkout (`company/ops/claims/`), so builders in separate worktrees see each other's claims. Built lessons are never handed out again, and a lock older than 6 hours is treated as abandoned.
- **Known-wrong briefs** are listed in `company/ops/brief-skips.json` and never handed out. Today that's fake-the-coin-flips, lighter-yet-boils-later and peak-is-not-the-end.
- **Lessons already in progress** were seeded as claims: 45 of them, read from the running agents' worktrees.
- **`--from-end`** lets a new builder take briefs from the end of a list while an older builder works forward without the queue.
- **Builders' instructions** now say to get all work from the queue. The chief-of-staff checklist covers how to run it, including re-seeding after a container restart.

With this in place I've added a ninth builder. It works from the end of the life sciences list, then probability, so two builders now share those domains safely.

**Expected:** about 435 more lessons... correction, about 75 more lessons in flight across the nine builders, which takes us to roughly 500 once they merge. Nine agents raises the chance of hitting the usage limit. If that happens, the locks keep anyone from redoing claimed work, and I'll resume them afterwards.

body:
I built 4 lessons, not 7. Only 15 geography briefs were unbuilt, and the first 11 were off limits, so 4 were left: #52, #53, #54 and #55. I checked the main checkout before each; none of the four existed. All four are status "review", with `company/reviews/<slug>/build.md` written.

Verification:
- Registry and `npm run check` pass with 0 warnings.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` and `NEXT_DIST_DIR=.next-w6geo npx next build` are clean.
- The QA contract passes on phone and desktop for all 4 (8/8). I reran ISS after the label fix and it passed again.
- The run does not appear to have left `tsconfig.json` modified (I ran `git checkout tsconfig.json`).

Commits (not pushed): 8c4a6f2 (farthest-place-from-you, iss-never-over-moscow) and 1341d19 (parallel-vs-arc-short-hop, two-distances-two-places). I used the commit message "Wave 6 geography: <slugs>" for each pair. `_scratch/` (my node scripts) is untracked and uncommitted. Nothing precomputed ships; every value is computed at runtime.

Lessons (all claims "unverified", with sources noted as from memory where they are):
- **parallel-vs-arc-short-hop** ("When does the shortcut pay?"): Mercator map with a parallel and a great circle, distance presets and slider, and a latitude cycle. Milestones: 1,000 km at 40N, 5,000 km at 40N, 5,000 km at 60N.
- **two-distances-two-places**: Equal Earth map zoomed on Europe, rings around Paris and Rome with crossings computed from the drawn radii, and a Madrid toggle. The start state is 600/400 km (no crossing), so a "Set the signal" button reaches the question's 1,000/800 km.
- **iss-never-over-moscow** (retitled "Where can the ISS fly over?"; the slug is kept): Equirectangular map with an idealised 3-lap orbit track. ISS 51.6 and polar 90 presets come first in DOM order. Milestones: tilt set to 51.6, and tilt raised to at least Moscow's latitude.
- **farthest-place-from-you** ("How far is as far as it gets?"): azimuthal equidistant map with a pin that moves between Madrid, Wellington and Quito, and a learner ring. Milestones: ring at 20,000 km and pin moved.

Corrections to the briefs, each found by recomputing with d3-geo and recorded in the claims:
- **#52:** the brief's shares of 1.95%, 5.7% and 8.7% are really 1.91%, 5.35% and 7.97%. The saving grows roughly with the cube of distance, not the square (0.72 km at 1,000 km, 5.83 km at 2,000 km), so the reveal says "five times the distance, over 130 times the saving".
- **#53:** with these coordinates Madrid is 602 km from the sea crossing and 1,804 km from the Austrian one, not 810 and 2,280. The code derives the Madrid ring radius from the crossings.
- **#55:** the brief says the 20,000 km ring "collapses to a point", but on an azimuthal equidistant map the antipode is the whole outer edge. The stage instead shows the ring's real length, which falls to 95 km at 20,000 km, and the reveal says the edge is one point stretched into a circle.

Screenshots I looked at: the phone explore view of all 4, the phone reveal of ISS, and the phone explore of ISS again after the fix. The first ISS view had overlapping London and Rome labels, so I offset the labels. Nothing else looked wrong.

Weak spots:
- In the shortcut lesson the "60°N" label overlaps Alaska.
- A map-text claim in two-distances ("near the Balearic Islands") rests on my reading of the coordinates, because the 1:110m data has no Balearic Islands.
- The ISS inclination and orbit period are cited from memory and need the fact-checker.

Next: the fact-checker verifies the claims, and evaluators run walkthroughs. The brief owner (cm-geography) should correct briefs #52, #53 and #55 for the errors above. I did not add a progress.md entry or board moves; the chief of staff should record this handoff.

body:
The three orgs are set up, each with its own space on the new second floor of HQ, and Kenji, our principal engineer, has been briefed.

| Org | People | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Life Hacks** | Tess (category manager) and Sana (safety reviewer) | New category, incubating, with 12 starter concepts in the curriculum |
| **Personalization** | Mateo (lead) and Ifeoma (learner-model engineer) | Waiting for your brief |
| **International** | Yuki (localization lead), localizers, and cultural reviewers including Amira | Localization standard drafted |

**Life Hacks:**
- **Starter concepts:** salt on ice, drying faster, resting meat, unit prices, caffeine and sleep, among others.
- **Independent safety review:** Sana reports to the evaluation steward, not to the category, so the people who want lessons shipped can't overrule her. Anything touching food, chemicals, heat, electricity, health or money goes through her.
- **Refuse list in the charter:** no chemical mixing, no medical or dosage tips, no electrical work, nothing that defeats a safety device, no legal or financial advice.
- **Activation:** the category becomes active only once Sana has passed its first 5 lessons.

**Personalization:**
- **Until your brief arrives:** the team collects questions in its handbook and builds nothing irreversible.
- **Guardrail already written down:** personalise for recall, never for time on the feed and never on demographics.

**International:**
- **Localization, not translation:**
  - numbers in the question and on the stage are recomputed when units change;
  - currency and examples are adapted;
  - someone from the region reviews the culture.
- **Locale re-checks:** facts that change by region (voltage, driving side, laws, southern seasons) are re-checked for each locale.

**HQ:** floor tabs switch between Floor 1 (lessons and the company) and Floor 2. Floor 2 has the Life Hacks office, Safety desk, Personalization, Learner model lab, International, Locale desks, Culture review and a lounge. I also fixed a small render warning in HQ.

**For Kenji (board W-089):** the decision record lists five engineering implications, and his open design review now carries a heads-up.
- **International:** locale variants make language a real axis in the storage design. That means a number and units layer in the kit (touching the lesson contract is a constitutional amendment), right-to-left scripts, and claims stored per locale.
- **Personalization:** it needs the backend, and its ordering logic must live outside lesson code, because lessons now run in the sandbox.
- **Life Hacks:** it may bring photos or video, which affects the per-lesson size budget.
- **Publish gates:** safety review and cultural review become new launch evidence. Wiring them into the gates is an amendment.

**First tasks on the board:**
- Tess writes the first 5 Life Hacks briefs.
- Yuki proposes the first locales.
- Your Personalization brief is listed as waiting on you.

**Meanwhile, lessons:** 442, after 4 more geography lessons merged. The geography-from-the-end builder found only 4 briefs it was allowed to take, and corrected three wrong geography briefs; the fixes are on the board. Five builders are still running.

**Screenshots looked at:** 10 of 10 on phone. Fixes I made from them: narrowed the histogram range (2), moved the dashed line off the text (3), shrank the grid so the reveal isn't clipped (4, 8), and shrank the readouts so "Profit" isn't cut off (6).

- 11c0442

- 457d488, the final commit, which includes the registry and the last CSS fixes.
- The final message carries the Opus 5.5 co-author line. The earlier four commit messages were not given a co-author line.
- tsconfig.json was restored.

**Design choices**
- Each reveal quotes only numbers from the learner's own run or from the same model function the stage draws.
- Reveals are gated with `<Milestones>` on states reachable through buttons; the slider is never the only way to reach the key state.

- Answer readouts show "?" while locked.

- a-birthday-like-mine: I replaced the ring of random birthday dots with exact bars plus comparison counts. A random crowd would show matches that disagree with the exact bars.
- real-effect-missed, selected-and-now-opposed, two-random-walks-agree: I added a better-test toggle, kept one line of text for r, and added "Show 30 more" respectively, so the key state is visible on the QA path.
- capped-doubling-game: the brief expected the running average to wobble around $5 to $30. It doesn't. Over 400 seed sets the average after 550 games has a median of $11.6, and my seed hits an early $8,192 that lifts it to $25.8. This is disclosed in the claims and the reveal says another run could be lower. For cm-probability: the brief's "sim mean about $20.4" is one sample of a heavy-tailed mean.
- selected-and-now-opposed: the stage correlation at the top 14% is -0.63 (216 dots), against -0.68 in the brief (20,000 dots). The reveal uses the stage figure.

**What I believe:** the numbers and gating are solid (about 90% sure), because they were recomputed from the same code that draws the stage. Two citations, Miller and Sanjurjo 2018 and Yule 1926 / Granger and Newbold 1974, plus Armitage et al. 1969, are recorded as "to be checked" and not verified.
